stem: A 13-year-old boy is undergoing anesthesia for an appendectomy. He receives propofol, succinylcholine, and fentanyl for induction. Propofol acts primarily at which of the following receptors?
explanation: Propofol acts on gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA) receptors. Propofol increases the time that the GABAA receptors remain open after activation. GABAA receptors, when active, allow Cl- to enter neurons and hyperpolarize the cell. Propofol is a useful induction agent because it produces a quick, reliable onset of general anesthesia. Several other medications target the GABAA receptor including etomidate and benzodiazepines. Benzodiazepines directly activate the GABAA receptor. Alpha2 receptors are prejunctional receptors activated by norepinephrine (negative feedback loop). Alpha2 receptors are agonized by clonidine and dexmedetomidine. Dexmedetomidine is much more selective for the alpha2 receptor than clonidine. Agonism of the alpha2 receptor causes sedation without respiratory depression. Side effects of alpha2 receptor agonism include hypotension and bradycardia. In some instances, a bolus of dexmedetomidine can cause hypertension because of the activation of the sympathetic nervous system.
rationales:
GABAB receptors are linked to potassium channels. The most common GABAB receptor agonist medication is baclofen. Baclofen is used to treat muscle spasticity from spinal and supraspinal pathology.
Answer C: The N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor contains a calcium channel inhibited by several medications. Ketamine is the prototypical anesthetic agent that affects the NMDA receptor. Phencyclidine (PCP) and nitrous oxide also antagonize the NMDA receptor. Antagonism of the NMDA receptor can cause anesthesia without producing respiratory depression. NMDA is also related to the development of chronic pain.
bottomLine: Propofol acts to potentiate GABAA receptors.
trueLearnInsight: To differentiate GABAA from GABAB, remember Baclofen for GABAB and Anesthetics for GABAA.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Propofol Mechanism Of Action" Miller, Ronald D. and Pardo, Manuel. Basics of Anesthesia. 6th edition. Propofol. Medscape.

stem: Which of the following will affect the onset of analgesia from local anesthetics the LEAST?

options.text: Addition of fresh bicarbonate to local anesthetic
options.html: Addition of fresh bicarbonate to local anesthetic

options.text: Addition of fresh epinephrine to local anesthetic
options.html: Addition of fresh epinephrine to local anesthetic

options.text: Local tissue inflammation where local anesthetic is administered
options.html: Local tissue inflammation where local anesthetic is administered

explanation: The addition of fresh epinephrine to a plain local anesthetic does not significantly change the block onset time. Local anesthetics are weak bases that bind to the intracellular portion of voltage-gated sodium channels and prevent nerve conduction. Although the “active” form of local anesthetics is the ionized form [charged cation (BH+)], the speed of onset of effect is determined by the proportion of local anesthetic in the unionized [basic, uncharged (B)] form. Unionized molecules pass through the lipid membrane and reach their targets easier than ionized molecules. The onset of action of local anesthetics is primarily a result of lipid solubility and pKa. The more lipid soluble, the more quickly the molecule can pass through the cell lipid membrane and reach its sites of action. The pKa of a drug refers to the pH at which the drug exists in equal parts of ionized and unionized forms. A local anesthetic with a lower pKa will have a greater unionized fraction (and generally faster onset) at physiologic pH (7.4) than a local anesthetic with a higher pKa (greater ionized fraction at physiologic pH and generally slower onset).
rationales:
Local anesthetics are formulated as hydrochloride salts with a pH slightly <7, as the ionized molecule is more soluble and stable than the free base. Once injected, the local anesthetic solution is quickly buffered to the pH of the tissue. The addition of bicarbonate to a local anesthetic mixture speeds the onset of action by raising the pH of the anesthetic solution so that more of the unionized fraction is available. Note that bicarbonate should only be mixed just prior to injection as the mixture becomes less stable for storage.
Answer B: Epinephrine causes local vasoconstriction, which prolongs the duration of effect of local anesthetics. By decreasing local blood flow, local anesthetic is maintained in the area of injection. Epinephrine solutions must be acidic (pH 2-5) to preserve the epinephrine. The addition of typical amounts of fresh epinephrine to plain local anesthetics (pH ~6) has little effect on the speed of onset of local anesthetics. However, premixed local anesthetic solutions with epinephrine are significantly more acidic (pH 3-4); this drives the local anesthetic to its ionized form, thus potentially slowing speed of onset.
Answer C: Local anesthetic concentration also affects the speed of onset. The greater the concentration, the faster the speed of onset since there is a steeper concentration gradient to drive local anesthetics intracellularly. This is how chloroprocaine (pKa 9, which would predict a slow onset) has such a rapid onset: a 3% solution is highly concentrated compared to, for example, 0.25% bupivacaine (pKa 8.1).
Answer D: Tissue inflammation slows the onset of effect of local anesthetics. Inflammation leads to a localized acidic environment. This drives more local anesthetic into its ionized form (local pH is farther from local anesthetic pKa), thus decreasing the speed of onset. Additionally, increased blood flow associated with inflammation washes local anesthetics away from their site of action.
bottomLine: The onset of effect of a local anesthetic is affected by its concentration (higher is faster), lipid solubility (higher is faster), pKa (lower is faster), and environment pH (higher is faster). Anything that increases the concentration or proportion of local anesthetic in its unionized form will speed the onset of analgesia.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Local Anes Onset: Factors Influencing" Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 914-916, 920, 924-925.

stem: Which of the following describes the mechanism by which the duration of action of rocuronium is prolonged when desflurane is used?

options.text: Blocked release of acetylcholine at the motor end-plate
options.html: Blocked release of acetylcholine at the motor end-plate

options.text: Decreased sensitivity of the postjunctional membrane to depolarization
options.html: Decreased sensitivity of the postjunctional membrane to depolarization

options.text: Reduced reuptake of acetylcholine at the motor end-plate
options.html: Reduced reuptake of acetylcholine at the motor end-plate

explanation: Volatile anesthetics decrease the sensitivity of the postjunctional skeletal muscle cell membrane to depolarization. This effect is more pronounced with longer duration of anesthesia as more volatile anesthetic is taken up by skeletal muscle.
rationales:
Volatile agents do not alter acetylcholine release.
Answer C: Acetylcholine is metabolized to acetate and choline in the neuromuscular junction and then choline is taken up by prejunctional neurons. Acetylcholine is not taken up prior to hydrolysis.
Answer D: Volatile agents may augment neuromuscular blockade by increased muscle blood flow via vasodilation, which may increase delivery of vecuronium to the muscle.
bottomLine: Volatile anesthetics potentiate neuromuscular blockade by DECREASING sensitivity of the postjunctional membrane to depolarization and INCREASING skeletal muscle blood flow which both augment neuromuscular blockade. In addition, potentiation of neuromuscular blockade occurs by depression of upper motor neurons.

stem: A 32-year-old obese female with bipolar disorder and hypertension is undergoing an elective gastric banding procedure. She takes simvastatin, lisinopril, and lithium. Which of the following statements about lithium is TRUE?

options.text: Lithium does not prolong blockade of either depolarizing or nondepolarizing muscle relaxants
options.html: Lithium does not prolong blockade of either depolarizing or nondepolarizing muscle relaxants

options.text: Lithium does not prolong the blockade of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants, but prolongs depolarizing blockade
options.html: Lithium does not prolong the blockade of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants, but prolongs depolarizing blockade

options.text: Lithium prolongs blockade of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants, but not depolarizing muscle relaxants
options.html: Lithium prolongs blockade of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants, but not depolarizing muscle relaxants

options.text: Lithium prolongs blockade of both nondepolarizing and depolarizing muscle relaxants
options.html: Lithium prolongs blockade of both nondepolarizing and depolarizing muscle relaxants

explanation: Lithium prolongs action of succinylcholine and non-depolarizing relaxants such as rocuronium and vecuronium. Lithium is a metal that, as a salt, is often used in the treatment of bipolar disorder and several other psychiatric conditions. Lithium is a cation with a charge of 1+. Lithium reduces excitatory neurotransmission while increasing GABA or inhibitory neurotransmission. Lithium has been shown to decrease acetylcholine release from alpha motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction. This causes lithium to prolong the duration of action of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents. Additionally, lithium activates potassium channels and thus inhibits neuromuscular transmission presynaptically and muscular contraction postsynaptically. The combination of lithium and nondepolarizing blockers results in a synergistic inhibition of neuromuscular transmission. The combination of lithium and succinylcholine results in additive inhibition.
rationales:
Antibiotics have different effects with regard to duration of neuromuscular blockade. Cephalosporins and penicillins do not affect neuromuscular blockade. However, aminoglycosides and clindamycin do have a significant effect on neuromuscular blockade.
Answer B: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency is a genetic autosomal recessive condition that affects the duration of depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents, but not most nondepolarizing agents. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency occurs in about 1 in 5,000 Caucasian individuals. Pseudocholinesterase is responsible for the metabolism of succinylcholine. Mivacurium is the only nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is metabolized by pseudocholinesterase, and therefore its duration of action is prolonged by pseudocholinesterase deficiency.
Answer C: Myasthenia gravis is a condition where nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers are prolonged. Depolarizing blockade in patients with myasthenia gravis is typically shortened because of the decreased number of receptors available for blockade. Succinylcholine works by binding to both alpha units of the acetylcholine receptor and causing activation. However, in myasthenia gravis many of the receptors are already occupied decreasing the efficacy of succinylcholine.

stem: A 68-year-old man is undergoing a hemicolectomy for colon cancer. He is induced with propofol, paralyzed with rocuronium (0.6 mg/kg), and maintained on 1% isoflurane. Rocuronium is not redosed, and neuromuscular blockade is allowed to wear off. Which of the following muscles will be the first to reverse?
explanation: The order of recovery from neuromuscular blockade after nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent administration is, from first to last, diaphragm > laryngeal muscles > corrugator supercilii > abdominal muscles > orbicularis oculi > geniohyoid > adductor pollicis. The corrugator supercilii is the most resistant to neuromuscular blockers, and among the choices provided it will be the first to regain muscle function. Corrugator supercilii monitoring is reflective of laryngeal muscle paralysis and may be used to assess for adequate intubating conditions. The response to neuromuscular blockade of muscle groups to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA) occurs at different rates. When NMBAs are administered, the first muscle groups to become paralyzed are the central muscles, such as the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles, with response of the peripheral muscles such as adductor pollicis occurring later. This response is quicker for the central muscles due to the greater amount of blood flow and, as a result, NMBA delivery. Due to the higher density of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, the diaphragm is relatively resistant to nondepolarizing NMBAs and recovers much more quickly than any other muscle group despite being one of the first muscles to be paralyzed. At times, the adductor pollicis will be inaccessible due to positioning during surgery; in this case, the facial muscles may be used to assess for adequate intubating conditions because their recovery from neuromuscular blockade correlates well with the recovery of other muscle groups. For example, the recovery of the corrugator supercilii muscle at the eyebrow correlates well with the recovery at the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles, and the recovery of the orbicularis oculi correlates well with the adductor pollicis. Despite these correlates, it may be rather difficult clinically to distinguish between the responses of the two facial muscles. After the arms become accessible, it is advised to place the neuromuscular monitoring system back on the adductor pollicis.
rationales:
The adductor pollicis is more sensitive than the corrugator supercilii to neuromuscular blockade. Because the adductor pollicis is the most sensitive to the blockade, recovery of function provided evidence of greater recovery of more resistant muscles such as the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles. Recovery to a train-of-four (TOF) ratio of ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis is recommended prior to extubation. A TOF ratio < 0.9 results in impairment of laryngeal muscles, pharyngeal muscles, and the response to hypoxia.
Answer C: The orbicularis oculi would recover after the rectus abdominis.
Answer D: The rectus abdominis would recover after the corrugator supercilii.
bottomLine: The recovery of the corrugator supercilii muscle at the eyebrow correlates well with the recovery of the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles. It is one of the first muscles to recover from neuromuscular blockade after the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles.

stem: Which of the following drugs is the MOST nonionized at physiologic pH?
explanation: Alfentanil has the lowest pKa of all of the listed drugs with a pKa of 6.5. At a physiologic pH of 7.4, approximately 89% of the drug will be in its nonionized form. Commonly, fentanyl is considered a short-acting opioid while morphine is considered long-acting. However, the elimination halflives of the two drugs are similar and, surprisingly, fentanyl’s is longer (~3-6 hours for fentanyl and ~2-3 hours for morphine). The duration of effect of opioids, unlike many other drugs, is not primarily determined by drug elimination, but more importantly, by lipid solubility. Morphine has a longer onset time and duration of action because it has a more difficult time crossing and then leaving the blood-brain (or blood-spinal cord) barrier due to a lower lipid solubility. By contrast, the more lipid-soluble fentanyl has a shorter onset and duration of action since it readily crosses, and leaves, the blood-brain barrier. The lipid solubility of an opioid is a prime determinant of the onset and duration of action of the drug as it affects how easily the drug is able to cross cellular (lipid) membranes. In addition to a drug’s chemical composition, one of the most important physicochemical characteristics relating to lipid solubility is the fraction of the drug that is in a nonionized form. Ionized drugs are polar and do not readily pass through cell membranes whereas nonionized drugs are significantly more lipid soluble (often 103-104 times more soluble). The pKa of a drug refers to the pH at which it exists in equal parts of ionized and nonionized forms. An opioid with a pKa less than physiologic pH (~7.4) will have a much greater nonionized fraction whereas an opioid with a pKa >7.4 will have a greater ionized fraction. The table below lists the lipid solubility, pKa, and percent of drug in a nonionized form at physiologic pH of the four opioids in this question. Lipid solubility is represented by the octanol-water partition coefficient (λow); the higher the λow, the higher the lipid solubility. A unique characteristic of alfentanil relative to other opioids is its significantly lower pKa resulting in a very high fraction of the drug existing in the nonionized form. Coupled with its moderate lipid solubility, this allows alfentanil to very rapidly cross the blood-brain barrier and have an ultra-short onset of action. The plasma-brain equilibration half-time of alfentanil is 0.9-1.1 minutes compared to 6.2 minutes for sufentanil, 4.7-6.4 minutes for fentanyl, and 139 minutes for morphine. Answers B & C & D: See table above.
bottomLine: Alfentanil has the lowest pKa and highest fraction of nonionized drug at physiologic pH.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Opioids: pKa" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 468-469, 484. Silverstein, Geriatric Anesthesiology, 2nd edition, pp. 211-213.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents to the intensive care unit in septic shock. She has type II diabetes, coronary artery disease, and chronic renal failure with a baseline creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL. Over the next 24 hours, she develops acute kidney injury and volume overload secondary to anuria with pulmonary edema and requires intubation for airway protection and mechanical ventilation. The plan is for intubation with neuromuscular blockade. Of the following neuromuscular blocking drugs, which will have the LONGEST duration of action for this patient?
explanation: Vecuronium is an intermediate-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drug (NMBD) that is primarily eliminated through the hepatobiliary system, but is partially cleared by the kidneys. Due to this, it has reduced clearance and increased half-life elimination in renal failure patients, likely due to build-up of a partially active metabolite 3-desacetylvecuronium. Renal failure does not affect the efficacy of NMBDs and initial dosing adjustments are not necessary, but renal failure does affect their clearance resulting in a longer duration of action. In general, it is best to avoid long-acting NMBDs, such as pancuronium. The commonly used intermediate-acting NMBD drugs, including cisatracurium, rocuronium, and vecuronium have important differences in duration of action in the setting of renal disease. Cisatracurium is degraded primarily by Hofmann elimination and its duration of action is unaffected by renal failure. Rocuronium's major route of elimination is the biliary system, but it is partially excreted unmetabolized in the urine. Because of this, the elimination half-life of rocuronium is slightly extended in renal failure; however, the duration of action of rocuronium has not been shown to be significantly different in renal failure patients in the clinical setting. Vecuronium's major route of excretion is also hepatobiliary, but it is secondarily cleared by the kidneys and has been shown to have an extended elimination half-life and an extended duration of action in renal failure patients. This is likely due to the buildup of 3-desacetylvecuronium, the primary metabolite of vecuronium, which has 80% of the neuromuscular blocking function of vecuronium and is excreted by the kidneys. The change in clearance and extended duration of action of vecuronium has been shown to have clinical significance in the intensive care unit (ICU) population. Succinylcholine is a short-acting depolarizing NMBD that has a half-life of fewer than 12 minutes in the absence of butyrylcholinesterase deficiency. Succinylcholine half-life is not prolonged in renal failure.
rationales:
Cisatracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination, which is independent of renal function, and is commonly chosen for use in patients with renal failure.
Answer B: Rocuronium is eliminated 70% by hepatic metabolism and only about 10% by renal elimination. It is generally considered safe to use in patients with renal failure with a minimal extended duration of action that is clinically insignificant.
bottomLine: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs (NMBDs) may be affected by renal disease. Of the commonly used intermediate-acting nondepolarizing NMBDs, vecuronium has the most prolonged duration of action in renal failure patients. Cisatracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination (independent of renal clearance) and the duration of action of rocuronium is largely unaffected by renal failure.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Renal Failure: Relaxants" Miller’s Anesthesia 9th Edition. Chapter 27: Pharmacology of Neuromuscular Blocking Drugs.

stem: The mechanism of mannitol MOST closely resembles the mechanism of which of the following conditions?
explanation: Mannitol is a sugar alcohol that acts as an osmotic diuretic as it is freely filtered at the glomerulus with poor reuptake back into the vasculature. Hyperglycemia may also act as an osmotic diuretic when glucose levels rise beyond the point of maximum transport through the glomerulus. Any poorly reabsorbed solute that is easily filtered at the level of the glomerulus can act as an osmotic diuretic by creating a gradient that causes fluid to remain within the renal tubule. Mannitol is the prototypical osmotic diuretic. Urea, glycerin, and isosorbide have also been used as osmotic diuretics. Mannitol draws fluid into the renal tubule, which allows for continued patency and flushing of debris from the tubule. Accordingly, mannitol can exert a renal protective effect. In addition, mannitol transiently creates an osmotic gradient within the vasculature and can maintain circulating plasma volume and renal perfusion via this effect, further eliciting protective properties.
rationales:
Angiotensin is part of the RAAS and is activated during systemic stress (e.g., hypovolemia, shock) to help retain fluid and maintain circulating plasma volume.
Answer B: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released in response to atrial stretch (generally due to volume overload). Atrial natriuretic peptide then induces diuresis via natriuresis, not via an osmotic effect. Atrial natriuretic peptide blocks the reabsorption of sodium from the distal tubule and collecting duct causing fluid to shift into the tubule.
bottomLine: Hyperglycemia can mimic the effects of mannitol by acting as an osmotic diuretic.
trueLearnInsight: Mannitol is relatively contraindicated in patients with congestive heart failure (CHF) due to an initial increase in intravascular volume. Furosemide is the drug of choice when diuresis is recommended in this class of patients.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Mannitol Osmolarity Effects” Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 1349-1350, 1359-1360. Evers, Anesthetic Pharmacology, 2nd edition, pp. 790, 795.

stem: A 48-year-old man with diabetes mellitus is scheduled to undergo renal transplantation for dialysis-dependent end-stage renal disease secondary to diabetic nephropathy. The patient also has a history of depression, for which he takes St. Johns Wort daily, which he is continuing to take until surgery. Which of the following is MOST likely true?

options.text: He will need higher doses of cyclosporine dosing
options.html: He will need higher doses of cyclosporine dosing

options.text: There is an increased risk of hypertensive crisis with the use of ephedrine
options.html: There is an increased risk of hypertensive crisis with the use of ephedrine

options.text: Warfarin therapy for postoperative anticoagulation will be enhanced with an increased risk of bleeding
options.html: Warfarin therapy for postoperative anticoagulation will be enhanced with an increased risk of bleeding

explanation: This patient is taking St. John's Wort which induces cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoenzymes and increases the metabolism of cyclosporine. This can result in subtherapeutic drug levels and an increased risk of transplant rejection. There have been case reports of acute transplant rejection in patients taking St. John's Wort for depression, and its use should be stopped at least five days before surgery and not restarted after surgery in these patients. St. John's Wort has been used by patients to treat depression, and its mechanism of action is related to the inhibition of serotonin reuptake, dopamine reuptake, and norepinephrine reuptake. Previous thoughts were that its action was similar to a monoamine oxidase (MAO)inhibitor; however, the in vivo relevance has been invalidated. Primary surgical and anesthetic concerns include induction of CYP 3A4 resulting in enhanced metabolism of drugs such as lidocaine, alfentanil, and midazolam as well as CYP 2C9, which is involved in the breakdown of warfarin. Warfarin therapy is, therefore, unreliable in patients taking St. John's Wort and puts them at risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and thromboembolism.
rationales:
St. John's Wort is not a substantial MAO inhibitor in vivo and therefore would not increase the risk of hypertensive crisis intraoperatively with the use of ephedrine.
Answer C: Warfarin breakdown will be enhanced and therefore the risk of DVT and thromboembolism will be increased.
bottomLine: St. John's Wort is an herbal antidepressant that induces the CYP enzymes and can alter drug responses with antirejection medications, warfarin, and intraoperative anesthetics. It should be stopped at least 5 days prior to any surgical operation.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Herbal Supplements" Miller's Anesthesia. Anesthetic Implications of Complementary and Alternative Medications in 8th edition. Pages 1226-1239. Barone GW, et al. Drug interaction between St. John's wort and cyclosporine. Ann Pharmacother. 2000 Sep;34(9):1013-6.
correctAnswerText: He will need higher doses of cyclosporine dosing
explanationHtml:
This patient is taking St. John's Wort which induces cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoenzymes and increases the metabolism of cyclosporine.

This can result in subtherapeutic drug levels and an increased risk of transplant rejection. There have been case reports of acute transplant rejection in patients taking St.

John's Wort for depression, and its use should be stopped at least five days before surgery and not restarted after surgery in these patients. St.

John's Wort has been used by patients to treat depression, and its mechanism of action is related to the inhibition of serotonin reuptake, dopamine reuptake, and norepinephrine reuptake. Previous thoughts were that its action was similar to a monoamine oxidase (MAO)inhibitor; however, the in vivo relevance has been invalidated.

Primary surgical and anesthetic concerns include induction of CYP 3A4 resulting in enhanced metabolism of drugs such as lidocaine, alfentanil, and midazolam as well as CYP 2C9, which is involved in the breakdown of warfarin. Warfarin therapy is, therefore, unreliable in patients taking St.

John's Wort and puts them at risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and thromboembolism.
rationalesHtml:
• Answer B: St. John's Wort is not a substantial MAO inhibitor in vivo and therefore would not increase the risk of hypertensive crisis intraoperatively with the use of ephedrine.

bottomLineHtml:

It should be stopped at least 5 days prior to any surgical operation.

stem: Following an induction dose of thiopental, which of the following MOST significantly contributes to the drug’s termination of action?
explanation: The termination of action of a bolus dose of thiopental is primarily due to redistribution of the drug from the brain to peripheral tissues (C). After injection of a single bolus dose of a drug, it distributes at different rates to tissues based on their relative perfusion (see figure below). Thiopental rapidly diffuses to the brain (within 30-60 seconds from injection) due to the high proportion of cardiac output that goes to the brain. In addition, thiopental is lipophilic and easily crosses the blood brain barrier. Due to the brain’s low relative volume, the concentration of thiopental within the brain quickly equilibrates with the plasma concentration. It is during this time period where thiopental exerts its greatest anesthetic effects. In addition to the brain, thiopental is also being taken up by other body tissues (e.g. muscle, fat) albeit at a lower rate due to lower relative perfusion. As this happens, the drug plasma concentration falls and the concentration gradient between the brain and plasma reverses. The drug in the brain rapidly diffuses back into plasma and is subsequently redistributed to all the other tissues still taking up the drug. In this way, redistribution of thiopental from the brain to other body tissues is the primary mechanism for the drug’s termination of action (C). It is not due to metabolism and elimination which occurs much more slowly (elimination half-time of 11 hours). Other examples of drugs whose terminations of action are primarily due to redistribution (following a single bolus dose) include methohexital, propofol, and fentanyl; all of these drugs are highly lipophilic. Metabolism of most drugs occurs via two processes, phase I and phase II metabolism. Phase I includes oxidative and reductive reactions including hydrolytic reactions and those catalyzed by the hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phase II reactions involve conjugation of the drug or its metabolite(s) with a substrate such as glucuronic acid. Once a drug is metabolized, it is much more efficiently eliminated from the body. During a prolonged thiopental infusion, peripheral tissue concentrations (e.g. muscle, fat) of the drug reach central compartment (blood and highly perfused tissues) concentrations and the termination of action of the drug becomes dependent on elimination by hepatic metabolism. The most important step in termination of action in this situation is side-chain oxidation (D). In the setting of large and prolonged thiopental dosing, a desulfurization reaction can occur which produces pentobarbital (A). Pentobarbital has long-lasting CNS-depressant activity and its production prolongs the effects of thiopental. A limited number of drugs, such as remifentanil, are primarily metabolized by ester hydrolysis (B) in the blood by plasma esterases. The termination of action of these drugs is due to this rapid metabolism instead of redistribution.
bottomLine: The termination of action of the effects of a bolus dose of thiopental is primarily due to redistribution of the drug from the brain to peripheral tissues rather than by metabolism. The same is seen with bolus doses of methohexital, propofol, and fentanyl.

stem: A 45-year-old man is currently being treated with a new diuretic for resistant hypertension. Since he started the new medication, he has had erectile dysfunction. Which of the following diuretics is the patient taking?
explanation: Spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic used to treat resistant hypertension, also has antiandrogenic effects that can lead to gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men. Potassium-sparing diuretics function at the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts. They consist of aldosterone receptor antagonists (spironolactone and eplerenone) and epithelial sodium channel blockers (triamterene and amiloride). Aldosterone leads to the synthesis and incorporation of Na+ channels and Na+/K+-ATPase into the distal convoluted and collecting duct cells. This results in increased Na+ absorption and K+ excretion. This process usually takes 24 to 48 hours, which is the reason antagonism of aldosterone takes time for its effect to be seen. Aldosterone receptor antagonists result in a mild natriuresis and retention of K+ by binding to aldosterone receptors, preventing the action of aldosterone. This also results in a decrease in H+ excretion. Side effects related to potassium-sparing diuretics include hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis. Additionally, spironolactone acts on sex hormone receptors acting as an antiandrogen. Because of the antiandrogen effects, additional side effects specific to spironolactone include gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men and amenorrhea in women.
rationales:
Amiloride shares many general side effects with spironolactone, such as hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis, but does not have antiandrogenic side effects.
Answer B: Side effects of furosemide include ototoxicity, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia.
Answer C: Side effects of hydrochlorothiazide include hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, hyponatremia, and hypomagnesemia.
bottomLine: Side effects related to potassium-sparing diuretics include hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis. Side effects specific to spironolactone include gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men and amenorrhea in women due to the additional antiandrogenic effect of spironolactone.
trueLearnInsight: The antiandrogenic side effects of spironolactone can be used clinically to treat androgenetic alopecia in women and moderate to severe acne vulgaris.

stem: Which of the following diuretics is NOT known to cause hypokalemia?
explanation: Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic and will not cause hypokalemia. There are several types of diuretics that are differentiated by the mechanism of action which occurs at different sites in the nephron; the prominent property of most diuretics is a reduction of sodium chloride reabsorption resulting in increasing sodium and water losses. Diuretics are used to treat a variety of pathologic states: hypertension, heart failure, renal dysfunction, glaucoma, and various other edematous states. There are several common adverse effects of diuretics: volume depletion, azotemia, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and acid-base disturbances. Volume depletion is most likely to occur at the start of treatment and it can result in depleted circulatory volume and reduction in tissue perfusion. Azotemia can occur from the decrease in renal perfusion resulting in an increase in BUN and creatinine (this is referred to as prerenal azotemia). Hyponatremia can occur, especially with thiazide diuretics, and is more common in patients with edematous states such as heart failure and cirrhosis. The major classes of diuretics include: Class Site of Action Mechanism of Action Examples Disease states diuretic is prescribed for Adverse effect Loop diuretics Thick ascending loop of Henle Inhibit the Na/K/Cl symporter driven by the Na gradient Increased urinary loss of Na, K, Ca, Mg and Cl Furosemide Torsemide Bumetanide Ethacrynic Acid Acute pulmonary edema Acute renal failure Heart failure Hypertension Hypercalcemia Alkalosis Hypocalcemia Hypokalemia Hypovolemia Ototoxicity Thiazide diuretics Distal convoluted tubule Inhibition of the Na/Cl cotransporter --> blocking NaCl reabsorption --> diuresis Hydrochlorothiazide Indapamide Metolazone Hypertension Heart failure Alkalosis Hypercalcemia Hypokalemia Hyperglycemia Hyperlipidemia Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors Proximal convoluted tubule Inhibit the activity of carbonic anhydrase inhibit the reabsorption of bicarbonate -> NaCl and NaHCO3 loss Acetazolamide Dorzolamide Edematous states Metabolic alkalosis Acidosis Bicarbonaturia Hypokalemia Nephrolithiasis Potassium Sparing Diuretics Collecting ducts and tubules Either inhibit the aldosterone receptor (spironolactone) OR block the Na channels (amiloride/triamterene) --> minor increase in urinary Na excretion and major decrease in urinary K Spironolactone Amiloride Triamterene Hyperaldosteronism Hypertension Heart failure Female hirsutism Diabetes insipidus Acidosis Hyperkalemia Azotemia Gynecomastia Nephrolithiasis Osmotic Diuretics Proximal convoluted tubule, thin descending loop of Henle, collecting ducts Inhibiting water reabsorption Mannitol Early stages of oliguria Brain edema Postischemic acute renal failure Pulmonary edema It is controversial whether mild hypokalemia caused by diuretics has any clinical significance; some believe it can increase the risk of sudden death and ventricular arrhythmias. Most agree that when mild hypokalemia becomes more profound, the risk increases significantly. Thus, when a patient is taking a diuretic known to cause hypokalemia, one must be cognizant of the potential for electrolyte disturbances in the perioperative period. This is particularly important when patients are fasting and given intravenous solutions which may be devoid of potassium. Answers B & C: These diuretics cause hypokalemia.
bottomLine: There are several different classes of diuretics, each having a different mechanism of action depending on where in the nephron they act. Hypokalemia can occur with several of the agents.
trueLearnInsight: Potassium-sparing mnemonic: The K+ STAys with spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Diuretics: Adverse Effects (B)" Pharmacology and Physiology for Anesthesia. 1st edition. Electrolytes and diuretics. Pages 608-611.

stem: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in which of the following patients?

options.text: A diabetic patient with gastroparesis having outpatient surgery
options.html: A diabetic patient with gastroparesis having outpatient surgery

options.text: A parturient presenting for emergency Cesarean section
options.html: A parturient presenting for emergency Cesarean section

options.text: A patient with a volvulus who last ate 2 hours prior to presenting to the hospital
options.html: A patient with a volvulus who last ate 2 hours prior to presenting to the hospital

options.text: A trauma patient presenting for splenectomy whose NPO time is unknown
options.html: A trauma patient presenting for splenectomy whose NPO time is unknown

explanation: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in patients with bowel obstruction. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist centrally and a cholinergic agonist peripherally. It is used perioperatively as an antiemetic. By promoting gastric emptying and increasing gastroesophageal sphincter tone, it may decrease the risk of pulmonary aspiration. It is typically given in doses of 5-10 mg IV 15-30 minutes prior to induction to allow sufficient time for drug onset. However, drug combinations involving metoclopramide are not found to reduce PONV to a greater extent than monotherapy. It may be because at dosages commonly used perioperatively (e.g. 10 mg), metoclopramide only has mild antiemetic effects. Higher doses (25-50 mg) may be necessary to have discernible benefit, but carry the risk of more side effects such as extrapyramidal symptoms. Metoclopramide has little effect on gastric acidity. Per ASA guidelines, "Metoclopramide is a weak antiemetic and at a dose of 10 mg is not effective in reducing the incidence of nausea and vomiting." As it is a promotility agent, risk of bowel perforation exists if metoclopramide is given to a patient with a bowel obstruction. Aspiration risk is best mitigated in these patients with rapid sequence induction with or without preoperative administration of intravenous histamine receptor antagonists.
rationales:
While ASA practice guidelines do not recommend routine use of gastric stimulants to compensate for patients who are not sufficiently NPO, several subsets of patients stand to benefit from promotility agents such as metoclopramide. Diabetic patients who may have some degree of gastroparesis, as well as anyone undergoing an outpatient procedure could be considered for metoclopramide use.
Answer B: During pregnancy, progesterone-mediated relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) occurs as early as the first trimester. Metoclopramide can counteract this relaxation of the LES and decrease gastric volume in a parturient. This medication could be considered as an antiemetic adjunct, especially in urgent situations where ideal NPO time may not be feasible though routine use has not shown reduction in the incidence of pulmonary aspiration.
Answer D: Similarly to the first two scenarios, any trauma patient should be considered full stomach secondary to unknown length of time since last oral intake with massive sympathetic output decreasing gastrointestinal motility. Metoclopramide could be considered to decrease the risk of pulmonary aspiration though decreased gastric fluid volume is not guaranteed.
bottomLine: Metoclopramide is a promotility antiemetic contraindicated in patients with complete bowel obstruction. Combinations involving metoclopramide are not found to reduce PONV to a greater extent than monotherapy. Metoclopramide is a weak antiemetic and at a dose of 10 mg is not effective in reducing the incidence of nausea and vomiting.
trueLearnInsight: Metoclopramide inhibits plasma cholinesterase and can increase the duration of action of succinylcholine.

explanation: There is high individual patient variability in pharmacokinetics for methadone dosing. The plasma half-life of methadone may range from 13 to 50 hours while the analgesic effects often last 4 to 8 hours. This high variability necessitates careful dose titration when starting a patient on methadone therapy to avoid dangerous side effects such as respiratory depression while providing adequate analgesia to patients. Methadone is a full agonist at mu receptors (it does also act as an NMDA receptor antagonist and as a monoamine transmitter reuptake inhibitor). stem: A patient undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy has received rocuronium for muscle relaxation at intubation. What is the mechanism of action for this medication?
explanation: Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (NDNMBs) act as nicotinic receptor competitive antagonists. Rocuronium is an NDNMB commonly used for muscle relaxation during surgery. Muscle contraction occurs through a series of steps. The presynaptic neuron first undergoes depolarization via an influx of sodium ions. Depolarization of the nerve triggers the influx of calcium into channels at the nerve terminal. Calcium facilitates the release of acetylcholine molecules out of the presynaptic nerve and into the neuromuscular junction. The acetylcholine molecules then bind to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the motor end plate, which leads to depolarization and then contraction of the muscle. Blocking the motor end plate acetylcholine receptor does not allow the muscle to contract. Because rocuronium is a competitive antagonist, its action can be overcome (in other words rocuronium can be displaced) by large numbers of the receptor agonist. This is the mechanism of neostigmine, the "reversal" agent. It is important to note that the term "reversal" does not imply antidote or a permanent (non-competitive) reversal. Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Acetylcholinesterase is the enzyme that degrades acetylcholine, and blocking this enzyme leads to increased numbers of acetylcholine molecules. The acetylcholine then displaces the rocuronium from the acetylcholine receptor, allowing muscle contraction. Neostigmine does not directly block the neuromuscular blockers or even directly block their effects. It reverses the paralysis indirectly by providing more agonist molecules to displace the neuromuscular blocker. If the neostigmine is given before enough of the NMB has been metabolized, there may still be too many molecules of NMB to adequately displace, and the patient will remain weak. They could alternatively appear strong initially only to weaken again later as the neostigmine is metabolized. This is the reason that NDNMBs must be carefully dosed and monitored with a nerve stimulator throughout surgery and with neostigmine administration. Unlike neostigmine, the drug Sugammadex is a selective relaxant binding agent (SRBA). Sugammadex is a modified γcyclodextrin, with a lipophilic core and a hydrophilic periphery. The negatively charged extensions electrostatically bind to the quaternary nitrogen of rocuronium as well as contribute to the aqueous nature of the cyclodextrin. Sugammadex's binding encapsulation of rocuronium is one of the strongest among cyclodextrins and their guest molecules. The rocuronium molecule bound within Sugammadex's lipophilic core is rendered unavailable to bind to the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Here are several ways to reduce the risk of residual blockade: 1) Use of clinical tests (head-lift, hand grip, etc.), but only useful for detecting severe blockade 2) Use of shorter-acting NDNMBs 3) Use of qualitative neuromuscular monitoring (tetanus, TOF count) 4) Use of quantitative neuromuscular monitoring (TOF ratio) 5) Routine reversal of neuromuscular blockade 6) Early reversal of neuromuscular blockade (not immediately at extubation) 7) Reversal at a higher TOF count 8) Avoidance of total twitch suppression 9) Use of new pharmacologic agents (Sugammadex)
rationales:
If Rocuronium was a non-competitive antagonist it could not be displaced by larger numbers of acetylcholine molecules and neostigmine would therefore not work as a "reversal" agent.
Answer C: Succinylcholine, a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, works as an acetylcholine receptor agonist.
bottomLine: All non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers act as competitive antagonists at the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
trueLearnInsight: Despite giving a patient an appropriate dose of neostigmine to “reverse” their neuromuscular blockade, it is still possible for a patient to remain paralyzed or weak, or to develop weakness later in the recovery room. This phenomenon is referred to as recurarization, and can occur after neostigmine wears off and the neuromuscular blocker (NMB) has not yet been metabolized or removed from the system. Residual neuromuscular blockade is defined as a train-of-four (TOF) ratio < 0.9 measured at the adductor pollicis muscle.

stem: Which of the following occurs with intravenous norepinephrine administration?

options.text: Decreased blood pressure with increased cardiac output
options.html: Decreased blood pressure with increased cardiac output

options.text: Increased blood pressure with a decrease in cardiac output
options.html: Increased blood pressure with a decrease in cardiac output

options.text: Increased blood pressure with cardiac output maintained or increased
options.html: Increased blood pressure with cardiac output maintained or increased

options.text: Increased heart rate and cardiac output
options.html: Increased heart rate and cardiac output

explanation: Administration of norepinephrine results in intense vasoconstriction and increasing blood pressure and, resulting in reflex bradycardia. This vasoconstriction on the venous system leads to effects that maintain cardiac output. The decreased venous capacitance causes an increase in venous return and preload. Although the heart rate has decreased, the increased preload along with the β1-stimulation (positive ionotropic effect) results in an increased stroke volume maintaining or slightly increasing cardiac output. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter released by postganglionic sympathetic neurons and has an affinity for the following: α1 > α2 > β1. Because of its affinities, administration of norepinephrine results in intense vasoconstriction (with reflex bradycardia) and increased myocardial contractility. As a result, norepinephrine primarily elevates arterial blood pressure without significantly affecting cardiac output.
rationales:
Isoproterenol is a nonselective β-agonist; its use leads to an increase in heart rate and cardiac output via β1 and a decrease in blood pressure via β2.
Answer B: Administration of pure α1-agonists such as phenylephrine leads to an increase in blood pressure through α1 vasoconstricting effects, resulting in reflex bradycardia. Unlike norepinephrine, there is no β1 activity increasing myocardial contractility; thus, cardiac output often decreases.
Answer D: Unlike epinephrine, administration of norepinephrine does not lead to tachycardia due to the intense vasoconstriction-mediated reflex bradycardia. Administration of epinephrine does lead to increased heart rate and cardiac output.
bottomLine: Administration of norepinephrine (α1 > α2 > β1) leads to intense vasoconstriction, causing slight reflex bradycardia. Despite the bradycardia, cardiac output is maintained via a decrease in venous capacitance, resulting in an increase in preload and stroke volume. The β1 increase in myocardial contractility further increases the stroke volume, and, despite a decrease in heart rate, cardiac output is maintained or slightly increased.

stem: A 21-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks gestation is receiving magnesium therapy for preeclampsia. At what serum magnesium level would you expect to begin to observe PR prolongation and QRS widening on an electrocardiogram?
explanation: Magnesium is commonly used in parturients as seizure prophylaxis for preeclampsia and as a tocolytic agent in pre-term labor as it causes tocolysis by relaxing uterine smooth muscle and vascular tone. ECG changes begin to occur when serum magnesium levels are between 7-12 mg/dL Normal serum magnesium levels are between 1.5-2.5 mg/dL. Hypermagnesemia is > 2.5 mg/dL and can result from kidney impairment, overuse of magnesium-based laxatives or enemas, over-infusion of magnesium in preeclampsia treatment, and disorders such as milk-alkali syndrome. Hypermagnesemia results in neurotoxicity by decreasing transmission of the impulse across the neuromuscular junction resulting initially in diminished deep tendon reflexes. As the magnesium levels rise (see table below), the reflexes disappear. Cardiotoxicity results from magnesium acting as a calcium and potassium channel blocker, disrupting cardiac function and leading to complete heart block and cardiac arrest (> 12 mg/dL). Due to its calcium channel blocker effects, magnesium can lead to hypotension, bradycardia, and ECG changes including prolonged PR interval and widened QRS. Treatment of hypermagnesemia begins by stopping the source of magnesium. If the patient is symptomatic, calcium gluconate can be administered. The elimination of magnesium can be further increased by adding a loop diuretic and increasing diuresis with normal saline. If the patient has renal failure, dialysis is indicated. Table listing the symptoms of hypermagnesemia according to the serum magnesium levels. Magnesium Levels (mg/dL) Symptoms 1.5-2.5 • Normal serum magnesium level
rationales:
A serum magnesium level of 1.5-2.5 mg/dL is considered to be the normal range of magnesium.
Answer C: A serum magnesium level of 12-15 mg/dL may lead to muscle paralysis, respiratory failure, and complete heart block.
bottomLine: Magnesium toxicity has multiple effects seen at different serum levels, most of which are caused by its action as a calcium channel antagonist. PR prolongation and QRS widening can be seen at serum magnesium levels of 7-12 mg/dL.

stem: Which of the following medications is LEAST likely to cause hyperkalemia?
explanation: Terbutaline causes potassium to shift intracellularly which can potentially cause HYPOkalemia. Terbutaline, along with other β2-agonists such as epinephrine, causes potassium to shift intracellularly as a direct effect of β2-receptor stimulation. Nonselective β-blockers can prevent this side effect of β2-agonists. Overall, this effect is generally shortlived. In obstetric patients given terbutaline infusions for management of preterm labor, potassium levels were found to return to baseline within 30 minutes of discontinuation of the infusion1. Numerous medications and medication classes can cause hyperkalemia either by direct or indirect effects. See the table below for examples. ACE = angiotensin converting enzyme, NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
rationales:
Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) that significantly decreases the release of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. Since aldosterone causes secretion of potassium (by stimulating the Na+/K+ pumps in the renal distal tubules and collecting ducts), inhibition of its effects can lead to hyperkalemia.
Answer B: Losartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) that has the same downstream effects on potassium (hypokalemia) as an ACEI
Answer C: Administration of mannitol can cause translocational hyperkalemia. Since mannitol is significantly hypertonic, intravascular administration causes water efflux from cells. Solvent drag then occurs by which intracellular potassium follows the water efflux and becomes intravascular. Over time, hypokalemia can occur with prolonged mannitol use as diuresis favors potassium loss.
bottomLine: Terbutaline and other β2-agonists can cause hypokalemia. Multiple medications and medication classes, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, nonselective β-antagonists, NSAIDs, and potassium-sparing diuretics, can cause hyperkalemia.

bottomLineHtml: Terbutaline and other β2-agonists can cause hypokalemia. Multiple medications and medication classes, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, nonselective β-antagonists, NSAIDs, and potassium-sparing diuretics, can cause hyperkalemia.

stem: The potency of an inhalational anesthetic gas can be estimated by knowing its solubility in which substance?
explanation: In the late 1800s, Charles Ernest Overton and Hans Horst Meyer independently observed a significant correlation between the potency of anesthetics and their solubility in olive oil. There are several theories of general anesthetic action. The Meyer-Overton correlation, also known as the lipid solubilityanaesthetic potency correlation, was part of a theory that related the fatty fraction in brain cells and anesthetic action. Although this has been useful for determining potency, it has not fully explained the mechanism of general anesthetics. Based on this correlation, another theory persisted for many years regarding hydrophobic anesthetic molecules accumulating inside the neuronal cell membrane, leading to membrane thickening and change in function. This theory was found to have several flaws. For example, stereoisomers of a volatile anesthetic have very different potency but their oil/gas partition coefficients are similar. Also, increases in body temperature can cause similar neuronal membrane changes without causing anesthesia. One of the issues with understanding the mechanism of anesthetics is the diversity of molecular structures between different anesthetics (e.g. chloroform, ethanol, ether, sevoflurane). This suggests to researchers that there is no specific structure-activity relationship, meaning there may not be a specific receptor that anesthetics are binding to. This led to the unitary hypothesis, which proposes that a common mechanism accounts for all anesthetic actions. A modern version of lipid hypothesis exists. With this theory, solubility of anesthetics in the lipid bilayer causes a redistribution of membrane lateral pressures. Other studies have shown that anesthetics can interact with proteins directly via hydrophobic binding sites, which can affect membrane proteins without interacting with the lipid bilayer. Regardless, the exact mechanism of general anesthetics remains unknown. Meyer-Overton correlation for the inert gases and nitrogen. Xenon is the most soluble inert gas in oil and thus the most potent. This is followed by krypton and argon. Answers A & B: The correct answer is olive oil.
bottomLine: The Meyer-Overton correlation related the potency of anesthetics with solubility in olive oil.
trueLearnInsight: The Meyer-Overton correlation led to the unitary hypothesis, which notes that a common mechanism accounts for all anesthetic actions.

stem: Which of the following is the mechanism of action for the negative inotropic effect seen with volatile anesthetics?

options.text: Decreasing the rate of dissociation of the γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor
options.html: Decreasing the rate of dissociation of the γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor

options.text: Increasing the permeability of the neuronal cell membrane to chloride ions
options.html: Increasing the permeability of the neuronal cell membrane to chloride ions

options.text: Reducing intracellular calcium in the myocardium
options.html: Reducing intracellular calcium in the myocardium

explanation: A reduction in myocardial contractility is seen with volatile anesthetics because of their ability to reduce calcium availability and/ or calcium sensitivity of the contractile apparatus. Volatile anesthetics affect both L-type and T-type calcium channels and depress contractile function by inhibiting sodium-calcium exchange, effectively reducing intracellular calcium concentration. Cardiovascular effects seen with volatile anesthetics include dose-dependent reductions in myocardial contractility, systemic vascular resistance, cardiac preload, and mean arterial pressure. Isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane depress myocardial contractility in vitro and in vivo. Desflurane causes systemic and coronary hemodynamic effects that are similar to those produced by isoflurane; however, cardiovascular stimulation can be seen with rapid increases in inspired concentrations of desflurane, which leads to transient increases in contractility from stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system. Cardiovascular effects of inhaled anesthetics Abbreviations: MAC, minimum alveolar concentration; SVR, systemic vascular resistance. *Can cause tachycardia at concentration >1 MAC.
rationales:
Decreasing the rate of dissociation of the γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor is the mechanism of action for barbiturates.
Answer B: Increasing the permeability of the neuronal cell membrane to chloride ions is one of the mechanisms of action for the sedative effects of propofol.
Answer C: Inhibiting intracellular sodium channels is the mechanism of action for local anesthetics.
bottomLine: Cardiovascular effects seen with volatile anesthetics include dose-dependent reductions in myocardial contractility, systemic vascular resistance, cardiac preload, and mean arterial pressure. The negative inotropic effect seen with the use of volatile anesthetics is mainly due to the reduction of intracellular calcium in the myocardium. While volatile anesthetics mainly act as cardiac depressants, cardiovascular stimulation can be seen with rapid increases in inspired desflurane concentrations, which leads to transient increases in contractility.
trueLearnInsight: The effect of volatile anesthetics on sodium-calcium exchange and reducing intracellular calcium concentrations may be particularly important in the neonatal myocardium, which, compared to the adult myocardium, may be more sensitive to the negative inotropic actions of volatile anesthetics.

stem: How can anaphylactic reactions be differentiated from anaphylactoid reactions in the clinical setting?

options.text: Anaphylactic reactions do not require sensitization to the allergen
options.html: Anaphylactic reactions do not require sensitization to the allergen

options.text: Mast cell tryptase will rise in anaphylactic reactions only
options.html: Mast cell tryptase will rise in anaphylactic reactions only

explanation: Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions are both histamine-mediated reactions with signs and symptoms that are clinically indistinguishable. An anaphylactic reaction is a type I hypersensitivity reaction, an immunoglobulin E-mediated (IgEmediated) allergic response, that causes mast cell degranulation and histamine release. Anaphylactoid reactions are drug reactions that cause uncontrolled histamine release by a mechanism not involving IgE. Clinical features of these reactions include urticaria, bronchospasm, angioedema, and venodilation causing hypotension and cutaneous flushing. Common intraoperative triggers of anaphylactic reactions include muscle relaxants, latex, and antibiotics. Common triggers for anaphylactoid reactions include protamine, IV contrast dye, opioids, d-tubocurarine, and thiopental.
rationales:
Anaphylactic reactions are IgE-mediated and therefore require a sensitizing exposure to an allergen prior to the triggering exposure.
Answer B: Anaphylactoid reactions are not IgE-mediated; rather, they result from direct stimulation of histamine release.
Answer C: Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions result from profound endogenous histamine release. Serum tryptase levels therefore rise in both reactions. One study of mast cell tryptase levels found that their presence favors an IgE-mediated cause but does not always distinguish between anaphylactoid and anaphylactoid reactions; thus, patients in whom mast cell tryptase concentrations are not increased still require skin testing.
bottomLine: Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions are clinically indistinguishable histaminergic reactions with different triggering mechanisms.

stem: A 68-year-old man is scheduled for elective carotid endarterectomy. His past medical history is positive for depression treated with fluoxetine 40 mg daily, and hypertension treated with lisinopril 40 mg plus hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. He took all of his medications earlier on the day of surgery. After induction of general anesthesia, the patient experienced hypotension refractory to multiple phenylephrine, ephedrine, and glycopyrrolate boluses. In addition to giving fluids, you decide to start an infusion with the goal of reversing hypotension while maintaining cardiac output. Which of the following would be MOST LIKELY to achieve these goals?
explanation: Norepinephrine is the most effective treatment for refractory hypotension that is caused by ACE-I. ACE inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) are usually withheld in the 24 hours prior to general anesthesia to prevent intraoperative hypotension. Furthermore, a recent study found that withholding ACEis or ARBs 24 hours before major non-cardiac surgery was associated with a lower risk of death and postoperative vascular events. In patients who continue ACEi/ARB, sometimes intraoperative hypotension can be refractory to first-line measures such as fluids, ephedrine, phenylephrine, and glycopyrrolate. In addition to preventing the direct actions of Angiotensin II, ACEis and ARBs decrease the response to catecholamines and the circulating levels of vasopressin. Because of this, many textbooks recommend the use of exogenous vasopressin as a treatment for ACEi/ARB-induced hypotension. On the other hand, a randomized clinical trial comparing terlipressin (a longer-acting vasopressin analog available in Europe) to norepinephrine found that although both agents corrected hypotension, terlipressin decreased cardiac output and gastric perfusion, and increased lactate levels, whereas norepinephrine restored blood pressure while maintaining cardiac output, with normal lactate levels, and without affecting gastric perfusion. Bolus doses of vasopressin are a relatively common for intraoperative hypotension associated with ACEi/ARB use. A typical vasopressin infusion for septic shock would be 0.03 units/min, so a 1 unit bolus of vasopressin would be equivalent to more than 30 minutes of a continuous infusion. Single bolus doses of 0.5 or 1 unit vasopressin are large doses with the potential to significantly decrease gastric perfusion and also decrease cardiac output. Both ACE-Is and ARBs act on the renin-angiotensin-system (RAS). Renin is secreted from the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney in response to sympathetic stimulation. Renin converts angiotensinogen, which is formed in the liver, to angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II in the lungs by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors, resulting in catecholamine secretion, aldosterone secretion, vasoconstriction, and anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secretion. With the blockade of catecholamines and vasoconstriction, and decreased uptake of water from the kidneys, induction of anesthetic can result in hypotension. As previously mentioned, norepinephrine is preferred for refractory hypotension in this setting.
rationales:
In this case, ephedrine has already been tried and found ineffective. Also, ephedrine infusions are generally not recommended due to tachyphylaxis (acute tolerance that develops with indirect-acting sympathomimetics due to depletion of endogenous catecholamines at nerve endings).
Answer B: Methylene blue can block the vasodilatory effect of nitric oxide by inhibiting guanylate cyclase. However, it is usually considered a last-line medication for vasoplegic shock. Also it is contraindicated in patients receiving SSRIs because it is a MAO inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome.
bottomLine: Intraoperative hypotension associated with perioperative continuation of ACEi/ARB therapy: IV hydration, phenylephrine, ephedrine, glycopyrrolate are the early treatments. Refractory hypotension can be reversed with either norepinephrine or vasopressin, but only norepinephrine will do so while maintaining cardiac output and gastric perfusion.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding metoclopramide?

options.text: It increases lower esophageal sphincter tone
options.html: It increases lower esophageal sphincter tone

explanation: Metoclopramide is used to treat gastroparesis, but has been utilized as nausea prophylaxis during surgery or with chemotherapy. It is a dopamine antagonist, which derives its anti-nausea effect from antagonizing dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the CNS. At higher doses it also blocks serotonin receptors, which can also contribute to its antinausea effects. In addition, metoclopramide is a peripheral cholinergic agonist and enhances the response to acetylcholine in tissues of the upper GI tract. This action causes accelerated gastric emptying, reduced gastric fluid volume, increased tone and amplitude of gastric contractions, and enhanced peristalsis of the duodenum and jejunum. It causes relaxation of the pyloric sphincter, however increases lower esophageal sphincter tone. It has no effect on gastric pH. Due to its anti-dopaminergic effect, metoclopramide should be avoided in patients with Parkinson disease. It also has a risk of causing extra-pyramidal side effects such as tardive dyskinesia. Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) include akinesia (inability to initiate movement), akathisia (inability to remain motionless or a feeling of severe restlessness), and muscle spasms such as torticollis (spasm of the neck) or oculogyric crisis (spasm of the eyes, typically upward). Treatment options include diphenhydramine and benztropine.
rationales:
Metoclopramide is a dopaminergic antagonist.
Answer B: Metoclopramide decreases gastric fluid volume.
Answer C: Metoclopramide accelerates gastric emptying.
Answer D: Metoclopramide has no effect on gastric pH.
bottomLine: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that causes increased gastric motility and increased lower esophageal sphincter tone.

stem: A 23-year-old man is undergoing general anesthesia for an inguinal hernia. Shortly following induction, the patient becomes hypotensive with increased peak airway pressures. Which of the following is MOST commonly associated with perioperative anaphylaxis?
explanation: Of the items listed, perioperative anaphylaxis is most commonly associated with exposure to neuromuscular blocking agents. Studies have indicated that neuromuscular blocking agents and antibiotics are the classes of drugs most associated with perioperative anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is the result of a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction. Antigens bind to IgE antibodies on mast cells and basophils. The activation of these cells causes a significant histamine release resulting in hypotension, bronchospasm, and urticaria. Anaphylaxis occurs in 1 in 10,000-20,000 anesthetics and is associated with a 3.4% mortality rate. Most reactions occur within 5 minutes of administration of the causative medication or agent. Anaphylaxis to induction agents and opioids is rare. Some agents are associated with histamine release which can be confused for anaphylaxis. Tryptase is released from mast cells when IgE activates them, thus measurement of tryptase levels may be helpful in suspected anaphylaxis. Tryptase levels increase rapidly during anaphylaxis but also fall quickly, as the half-life is only 2 hours. Neuromuscular blockers are one of the most common agents associated with anaphylaxis (along with antibiotics). The incidence of anaphylaxis is thought to be 1 in 6,500, but this may be underreported. Quaternary ammonium ions found in NMB are the most likely culprit for causing IgE activation. Many household chemicals share similar quaternary ammonium to neuromuscular blocking drugs. Previous exposure to cough medicines containing pholcodine (previously used in Europe) has been associated with rocuronium anaphylaxis. Additionally, quaternary ammonium can be found in shampoo, soap, and toothpaste.
rationales:
Latex is a common allergen that may cause anaphylaxis. Latex often causes symptoms of anaphylaxis 30-60 minutes after exposure. However, anaphylaxis may occur immediately. People at higher risk of latex allergy include healthcare workers, atopic patients, and patients with spina bifida.
Answer B: Reactions to local anesthetics are rare but often suggested as a cause of anaphylaxis. Amino ester anesthetics are degraded into the metabolite para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA). PABA is the reason for reactions to most local anesthetics. Anaphylaxis to amino amide anesthetics occurs at an even lower frequency than amino ester anesthetics. Methylparaben, a common preservative, is often found in local anesthetics. Methylparaben is structurally similar to PABA, and therefore cross reactivity is possible. explanationHtml:
Of the items listed, perioperative anaphylaxis is most commonly associated with exposure to neuromuscular blocking agents. Studies have indicated that neuromuscular blocking agents and antibiotics are the classes of drugs most associated with perioperative anaphylaxis.

Anaphylaxis is the result of a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction. Antigens bind to IgE antibodies on mast cells and basophils.

The activation of these cells causes a significant histamine release resulting in hypotension, bronchospasm, and urticaria. Anaphylaxis occurs in 1 in 10,000-20,000 anesthetics and is associated with a 3.4% mortality rate.

Most reactions occur within 5 minutes of administration of the causative medication or agent. Anaphylaxis to induction agents and opioids is rare.

Some agents are associated with histamine release which can be confused for anaphylaxis. Tryptase is released from mast cells when IgE activates them, thus measurement of tryptase levels may be helpful in suspected anaphylaxis.

Tryptase levels increase rapidly during anaphylaxis but also fall quickly, as the half-life is only 2 hours. Neuromuscular blockers are one of the most common agents associated with anaphylaxis (along with antibiotics).

The incidence of anaphylaxis is thought to be 1 in 6,500, but this may be underreported. Quaternary ammonium ions found in NMB are the most likely culprit for causing IgE activation.

stem: Which of the following is MORE common with patient-controlled analgesia compared to nurse-administered bolus dosing of opioids for the control of postoperative pain?
explanation: Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) has a higher rate of pruritus compared to nurse-administered bolus doses of opioids for postoperative pain control. Patient-controlled analgesia is a relatively new technique that is made possible by sophisticated computer chip technology. Safety measures are programmed into the pump to prevent overdose that could cause death. In essence, PCA is an on-demand, intermittent administration of an opioid medication that is under the patient's control. The system can be set with or without a basal (continuous) rate, depending on patient characteristics and requirements. The provider sets several variables: the demand (bolus) dose, lockout interval (delay between doses), and, possibly, a background infusion (basal) rate. Several opioids have been used in PCA; commonly, hydromorphone, morphine, and fentanyl are used. Background rates were thought to improve analgesia; however, results of several studies have provided evidence that PCA increases the total dosage used and increases the risk of respiratory depression. Generally, basal rates are reserved for opioidtolerant patients. The incidence of opioid-related side effects other than pruritis from PCA vs intermittent dosing does not appear to differ significantly. The rate of respiratory depression is low for PCA without basal dosing (<0.5%) and is no different from intermittent or neuraxial opioid administration. Usually, respiratory depression is caused by errors in programming or administration (ie, operator error). Additionally, the rate of nausea, vomiting, sedation, and confusion are similar between PCA and intermittent dosing. The risk of pruritus was found to be higher in PCA dosing.
rationales:
Patient-controlled analgesia provides slightly improved analgesia and patient satisfaction; however, patients using PCA use slightly more opioids compared with those receiving bolus doses given by nursing staff.
Answer C: The rate of respiratory depression is low for PCA without basal dosing (<0.5%) and is no different from intermittent or neuraxial opioid administration.
bottomLine: The incidence of opioid-related side effects other than pruritis from PCA vs intermittent dosing does not seem to differ significantly.

stem: A 46-year-old male with a history of cirrhosis secondary to alcoholism presents for colectomy. He weighs 60 kg with a BMI of 19 kg/m2. General anesthesia is induced and a muscle relaxant is used for paralysis. Which of the following is TRUE in regards to neuromuscular blocking agents in this patient?

options.text: Cisatracurium will have a prolonged duration of action
options.html: Cisatracurium will have a prolonged duration of action

options.text: Intubating dose of rocuronium should be increased
options.html: Intubating dose of rocuronium should be increased

options.text: Succinylcholine duration of action will be prolonged to an average of 45 minutes
options.html: Succinylcholine duration of action will be prolonged to an average of 45 minutes

options.text: Vecuronium clearance will be increased due to decreased protein binding
options.html: Vecuronium clearance will be increased due to decreased protein binding

explanation: The intubating dose of rocuronium should be increased secondary to an increase in the volume of distribution of the drug. Neuromuscular blocking agents are highly water-soluble due to quaternary amine structures and thus an increase in body water, such as with cirrhosis, CHF, or renal failure, results in decreased plasma concentration of neuromuscular blockers requiring an increase in intubating dose. It is important to remember, however, that clearance of drugs dependent on hepatic metabolism is reduced and therefore they will have a prolonged duration of action. Rocuronium, vecuronium, and pancuronium will all have increased duration of action secondary to impaired hepatic metabolism (caveat: rocuronium is not metabolized but is cleared by the liver in the bile) and therefore maintenance dosing should be reduced and neuromuscular monitoring carefully followed.
rationales:
Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination in the plasma and thus the duration of action is not affected by cirrhosis or renal disease. A breakdown product, laudanosine, is cleared by the liver but levels produced are insignificant clinically.
Answer C: Succinylcholine is metabolized in the plasma by pseudocholinesterase and the duration of action is prolonged with severe liver disease secondary to decreased pseudocholinesterase production. This is rarely of clinical significance unless used in a very short procedure as the apnea time is increased from 3 minutes to 9 minutes.
Answer D: Vecuronium is metabolized and cleared by the liver, thus clearance will be decreased. Liver disease decreases plasma protein concentration and results in an increase in free drug concentration. This would normally increase drug clearance, however the impaired ability of the liver to metabolize the drug outweighs the decreased plasma protein concentration and thus duration of action is prolonged.
bottomLine: Intubating doses of neuromuscular blocking drugs are increased in cirrhosis because of the increase in volume of distribution. Maintenance doses of hepatically metabolized and/or cleared drugs should be reduced and neuromuscular function carefully monitored as duration of action is prolonged.

stem: Which of the following inhalational anesthetics decreases blood pressure primarily by decreasing cardiac output?
explanation: Halothane decreases systemic blood pressure mainly by reducing cardiac output. A common effect of potent volatile anesthetics is dose-related decreases in arterial blood pressure. It is well documented that sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane decrease arterial blood pressure, systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and myocardial function comparably and in a dose-dependent manner. The drop in blood pressure caused by these agents is directly related to the decrease in SVR while cardiac output is relatively maintained. Nitrous oxide, in comparison, generally leads to no change or an increase in arterial blood pressure. Halothane decreases arterial blood pressure primarily by decreasing cardiac output. Halothane causes minimal changes to SVR. Answers A & B & C: The drop in blood pressure caused by these agents is directly related to the decrease in SVR while cardiac output is relatively maintained.
bottomLine: Sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane decrease arterial blood pressure, SVR, and myocardial function comparably and in a dose-dependent manner. Halothane decreases blood pressure primarily by decreasing cardiac output and causes minimal changes to SVR.
trueLearnInsight: Halothane is unlikely to be tested on the current American Board of Anesthesiologists exams. However, understanding the other volatile anesthetics allows for this question to be answered. Additionally, some physicians being trained in the U.S. travel for medical mission work to areas of the world where halothane is more commonly used.
