stem: Which of the following is TRUE of somatic motor neurons and the neuromuscular junction?

options.text: Lower motor neurons originate in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord or in the motor nuclei of cranial nerves
options.html: Lower motor neurons originate in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord or in the motor nuclei of cranial nerves

options.text: Nicotinic muscle-type acetylcholine receptors consist of six protein subunits
options.html: Nicotinic muscle-type acetylcholine receptors consist of six protein subunits

options.text: Terminal nerve fibers at the neuromuscular junction do not have a myelin sheath
options.html: Terminal nerve fibers at the neuromuscular junction do not have a myelin sheath

options.text: The innervation ratio (the number of muscle fibers each neuron innervates) is consistent across all skeletal muscle groups in the body
options.html: The innervation ratio (the number of muscle fibers each neuron innervates) is consistent across all skeletal muscle groups in the body

explanation: Somatic motor neurons are myelinated, fast-conducting nerves. As the nerve axons progress to nerve endings, the myelin sheath is lost before branching into the terminal fibers. Each terminal fiber supplies a muscle fiber via the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). The NMJ consists of the presynaptic motor neuron nerve terminal and its Schwann cells, the synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic muscle fiber. Lower motor neuron cell bodies are located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord or in the motor nuclei of cranial nerves. The axons travel via the ventral roots to muscles. The axons end as terminal fibers at the NMJ. When an action potential reaches the nerve terminal, sodium from outside the nerve terminal flows inside. This depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, which allows the entry of calcium ions into the nerve terminal and causes acetylcholine to be released into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine then binds to the nicotinic muscle-type acetylcholine receptors, leading to an influx of sodium ions into the muscle and an efflux of potassium out of the muscle, causing depolarization and resulting in muscle contraction. Before birth, each muscle cell has contact with several nerves and has several NMJs. However, after birth, all but one of the nerves retract, and only one NMJ remains. A motor unit consists of the motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates. The innervation ratio is the number of muscle fibers that each neuron innervates. The innervation ratio changes depending on the function of the muscle group. For groups that require fine control, such as eye or facial muscles, the innervation ratio is 1:2 (one nerve innervating two muscle fibers). For large muscles with coarse, powerful movements, such as the thigh or back, the innervation ratio is much higher, approaching 1:2,000. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptors of muscle fibers are highly concentrated at the synapses. At birth, these receptors are immature and consist of five protein subunits (α2βγδ). After birth, the receptors mature by replacing the γ subunit with an ε subunit. Outside of the junctional area, there are far fewer receptors.

Lower motor neurons originate in the ventral horn of the spinal cord or the motor nuclei of cranial nerves. The dorsal horn contains the ascending sensory pathways and interneurons that make connections within the spinal cord.

Each terminal fiber supplies a muscle fiber via the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). The NMJ consists of the presynaptic motor neuron nerve terminal and its Schwann cells, the synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic muscle fiber.

Lower motor neuron cell bodies are located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord or in the motor nuclei of cranial nerves. The axons travel via the ventral roots to muscles.

The axons end as terminal fibers at the NMJ. When an action potential reaches the nerve terminal, sodium from outside the nerve terminal flows inside.

This depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, which allows the entry of calcium ions into the nerve terminal and causes acetylcholine to be released into the synaptic cleft.

Acetylcholine then binds to the nicotinic muscle-type acetylcholine receptors, leading to an influx of sodium ions into the muscle and an efflux of potassium out of the muscle, causing depolarization and resulting in muscle contraction. After birth, the receptors mature by replacing the γ subunit with an ε subunit. Outside of the junctional area, there are far fewer receptors.

stem: A 50-year-old man is started on spironolactone to treat secondary hyperaldosteronism. What side effect of the drug is he MOST likely to experience?
explanation: Spironolactone is a competitive aldosterone antagonist that is a potassium-sparing diuretic. It works in the distal tubule of the nephron segments in the kidney. Inhibition of aldosterone will cause a mild retention of potassium and excretion of sodium. The most commonly described side effects of spironolactone are hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, gynecomastia, and impotence. Other potassium sparing diuretics, such as eplerenone, triamterene, and amiloride, all possess similar side effects as spironolactone.
rationales:
Spironolactone may be added to a medical regimen to treat edema, specifically in those with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, or nephrotic syndrome. It is not likely to cause edema. In fact, spironolactone improves survival in patients with volume overload and heart failure.
Answer B: Spironolactone may be added to a medical regimen to treat hypokalemia. It is not likely to cause it. Instead, hyperkalemia and hyperkalemic, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis are more likely to occur.
bottomLine: The most commonly described side effects of spironolactone are hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, gynecomastia, and impotence.

stem: A 65-year-old man in the intensive care unit is hypertensive after a three-vessel coronary artery bypass graft, and a nicardipine infusion is started. Which of the following BEST describes how nicardipine lowers blood pressure?
explanation: Just as with all calcium channel blockers (CCB), nicardipine predominantly causes arteriolar vasodilation compared to venous vasodilation, resulting in decreased arterial blood pressure. Calcium channel blockers inhibit the firing of L-type voltagedependent Ca2+ channels. Calcium channel blockers can be generally divided into two chemical groups with unique pharmacodynamic profiles: dihydropyridine-type CCB (eg, nifedipine, nicardipine, nimodipine, clevidipine) and nondihydropyridine-type CCB (diltiazem and verapamil). Both groups of CCBs reduce left ventricular afterload and maintain preload because they preferentially dilate the arterial smooth muscle compared to venous smooth muscle, but dihydropyridine-type CCBs do not have a negative inotropic or dromotropic effect on the heart, while the nondihydropyridine-type CCBs have a negative inotropic and dromotropic effect on the heart. Calcium channel blockers are particularly useful for postoperative coronary artery bypass graft patients because they cause coronary arterial vasodilation and inhibit coronary artery vasospasm. These actions may enhance coronary blood flow if it is assumed that coronary perfusion pressure is not substantially reduced due to arterial vasodilation. Nondihydropyridine CCBs reduce myocardial oxygen demand by decreasing both heart rate and contractility. On the other hand, dihydropyridines may increase myocardial oxygen demand via reflex tachycardia, but they do not have a negative inotropic effect.
rationales:
Sodium nitroprusside causes both arterial and venous dilation, resulting in a decreased afterload and preload. Because of its rapid onset, sodium nitroprusside is frequently used in a hypertensive emergency.
Answer C: Diltiazem predominantly decreases chronotropy through inhibition at the level of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Diltiazem also decreases inotropy but to a lesser degree.
Answer D: Nitroglycerin is predominantly a venodilator, which results in a decreased preload. Decreased preload is useful in patients with decompensated heart failure from ischemia because it reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Patients with hypovolemic or inferior myocardial infarction should not be treated with nitroglycerin because it may result in dramatic hypotension.

Calcium channel blockers predominantly cause arteriolar vasodilation compared to venous vasodilation, resulting in decreased arterial blood pressure. Dihydropyridine-type CCBs do not have a negative inotropic or dromotropic effect on the heart, while nondihydropyridine-type CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) have a negative inotropic and dromotropic effect on the heart.

stem: Intraoperative administration of a calcium channel blocker to a naïve patient will MOST likely cause which of the following interactions with neuromuscular blocking drugs?

options.text: Mild augmentation of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing agents
options.html: Mild augmentation of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing agents

options.text: Mild augmentation of depolarizing agents and no effect on nondepolarizing agents
options.html: Mild augmentation of depolarizing agents and no effect on nondepolarizing agents

options.text: No effect on depolarizing agents and mild augmentation of nondepolarizing agents
options.html: No effect on depolarizing agents and mild augmentation of nondepolarizing agents

options.text: No effect on depolarizing agents and mild attenuation of nondepolarizing agents
options.html: No effect on depolarizing agents and mild attenuation of nondepolarizing agents

explanation: Concurrent administration of neuromuscular blocking drugs (NBDs) and calcium channel blockers (CCBs) to a CCB-naïve patient can cause mild potentiation of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs. Calcium ions play important roles in both smooth and skeletal muscle contraction. Calcium channel blockers alter calcium’s ability to cross the cellular membrane resulting in less excitation-contraction. Most studies examining this effect on skeletal muscle have been conducted with animal models and have revealed that CCBs cause a progressive dose-related reduction in twitch height. Additional studies (again, primarily in animal models or in-vitro) have examined the interactions of CCBs and NBDs. Most studies show the effects of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs muscle relaxants are augmented by CCBs. The exact mechanism behind this is unclear but it may be due to one or more of the following: alterations in presynaptic variables reducing calcium conduction, alteration of intracellular calcium pools, or inhibition of the calcium membrane pump mechanisms. All of these could result in a decrease of acetylcholine mobilization and modification of muscle relaxation. Additionally, there are case reports of patients who were given CCBs for cardiovascular disease in the perioperative period and then had severe weakness after muscle relaxation was administered. Given the information discussed above, careful titration of NBDs should be considered when given to patients who are also being administered CCBs in the perioperative period. Note that CCBs, when taken chronically, have only a very mild minor potentiation effect on both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs (generally only observed in in-vitro or animal study models). This effect is considered to be clinically insignificant and no changes in dosing to CCBs or NBDs are generally necessary. Answers B & C & D: Concurrent administration of NBDs and CCBs to a CCB-naïve patient can cause mild augmentation of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs.
bottomLine: Calcium channel blockers can augment depolarizing and nondepolarizing muscle relaxants, particularly when the two drugs are administered concurrently to CCB-naïve patients. Consider the careful titration of NBDs in this setting. In patients taking chronic CCBs, the augmentation effect is clinically insignificant.
trueLearnInsight: During treatment of malignant hyperthermia, CCBs should not be given in combination with dantrolene because it can lead to life-threatening hyperkalemia and myocardial depression. However, if a patient on a chronic CCB develops malignant hyperthermia, dantrolene should always be given as withholding dantrolene can significantly worsen mortality.

stem: Which of the following side effects can be seen with neostigmine administration?
explanation: Diarrhea is a side effect of the administration of the anticholinesterase agent neostigmine. The primary side effects of anticholinesterase administration are bradycardia and increased gastrointestinal activity. Glycopyrrolate is an antimuscarinic that can be administered before neostigmine administration to block the effects of neostigmine at muscarinic sites. Neostigmine is an anticholinesterase that functions by increasing the amount of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by competitively inhibiting cholinesterase. Neostigmine increases acetylcholine, which competes with nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking (NMB) agents for nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Neostigmine is often the preferred anticholinesterase used for reversal because of its quick onset of action, strong affinity for the cholinesterase enzyme, and fewer muscarinic side effects compared with other agents. It is a common reversal agent for NMB, but its use for reversal is declining with the rise of the use of sugammadex for the reversal of rocuronium and vecuronium. Because neostigmine blocks cholinesterase found at nicotinic and muscarinic sites, the addition of an antimuscarinic agent such as atropine or glycopyrrolate is used to prevent the side effects of bradycardia, nausea, increased peristalsis, and diarrhea. Other side effects of neostigmine include complete heart block, asystole, and bronchoconstriction. It is important to note that neostigmine does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
rationales:
Anhidrosis is an anticholinergic side effect, not a side effect of neostigmine.
Answer C: Mydriasis is an anticholinergic side effect, not a side effect of neostigmine.
Answer D: Urinary retention is an anticholinergic side effect, not a side effect of neostigmine.
bottomLine: Neostigmine competitively inhibits cholinesterase enzymes found at nicotinic and muscarinic sites, which increases the amount of acetylcholine. The addition of an antimuscarinic such as atropine or glycopyrrolate is used to prevent the side effects of bradycardia, nausea, increased peristalsis, and diarrhea caused by neostigmine administration.

The mnemonic correlates with the following symptoms: flushing, anhidrosis, dry mucous membranes, mydriasis, altered mental status, hyperthermia, and urinary retention.

stem: Which of the following groups of patients is LEAST likely to have an exaggerated increase in serum potassium following succinylcholine administration?

options.text: Major trauma patients >24 hours following injury
options.html: Major trauma patients >24 hours following injury

explanation: Although patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) may have higher baseline serum potassium concentrations than healthy patients, ESRD by itself does not affect the rise in potassium following succinylcholine administration. Transient serum potassium elevation is a side effect of succinylcholine due to skeletal muscle depolarization, which leads to cation influx and potassium efflux. In healthy patients, succinylcholine can transiently raise serum potassium as much as 0.5 mEq/L as a result of this potassium efflux. Patients with certain conditions can experience more profound succinylcholineinduced hyperkalemia (serum potassium increase up to nearly 3.5 mEq/L) due to nicotinic extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor upregulation. This can lead to cardiac arrhythmias and potential cardiac arrest. Answers A & C: Patient populations at risk for more profound succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia include those who are >24 hours status post burn injuries, major denervation injuries, peripheral denervation, spinal cord transection, or trauma that leads to prolonged immobilization. It is still appropriate to use succinylcholine to safely secure the airway in these patients if their injury is < 24 hours old, as there has not been enough time to experience nicotinic extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor upregulation.
rationales: Succinylcholine has a Black Boxed warning specifically for this reason. Caution should also be used in patients with muscular dystrophies (especially in children who can have potentially undiagnosed disorders), stroke patients, patients with neuromuscular disorders, or intensive care patients with prolonged immobilization. In some patients, such as muscular dystrophy, hyperkalemia can occur secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Other patients are also subject to upregulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors and are therefore more prone to significant succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia.
bottomLine: Succinylcholine administration transiently raises serum potassium approximately 0.5 mEq/L in healthy patients. Succinylcholine is contraindicated in patients with neuromuscular disorders, prolonged immobility, and those >24 hours status post burns, trauma, or denervation injuries. This is due to an upregulation of extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, leading to an increase in serum potassium up to 3.5 mEq/L following succinylcholine administration. In children, there is a risk of cardiac arrest from hyperkalemia rhabdomyolysis.

Transient serum potassium elevation is a side effect of succinylcholine due to skeletal muscle depolarization, which leads to cation influx and potassium efflux. In healthy patients, succinylcholine can transiently raise serum potassium as much as 0.5 mEq/L as a result of this potassium efflux.

Patients with certain conditions can experience more profound succinylcholineinduced hyperkalemia (serum potassium increase up to nearly 3.5 mEq/L) due to nicotinic extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor upregulation. This can lead to cardiac arrhythmias and potential cardiac arrest.

Answers A & C: Patient populations at risk for more profound succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia include those who are >24 hours status post burn injuries, major denervation injuries, peripheral denervation, spinal cord transection, or trauma that leads to prolonged immobilization.

It is still appropriate to use succinylcholine to safely secure the airway in these patients if their injury is < 24 hours old, as there has not been enough time to experience nicotinic extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor upregulation.
rationalesHtml: • Succinylcholine has a Black Boxed warning specifically for this reason. Caution should also be used in patients with muscular dystrophies (especially in children who can have potentially undiagnosed disorders), stroke patients, patients with neuromuscular disorders, or intensive care patients with prolonged immobilization. In some patients, such as muscular dystrophy, hyperkalemia can occur secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Other patients are also subject to upregulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors and are therefore more prone to significant succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia.
bottomLineHtml:
Succinylcholine administration transiently raises serum potassium approximately 0.5 mEq/L in healthy patients. Succinylcholine is contraindicated in patients with neuromuscular disorders, prolonged immobility, and those >24 hours status post burns, trauma, or denervation injuries.

This is due to an upregulation of extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, leading to an increase in serum potassium up to 3.5 mEq/L following succinylcholine administration. In children, there is a risk of cardiac arrest from hyperkalemia rhabdomyolysis.

stem: A patient receives local anesthetic subcutaneous infiltration and develops urticaria. Upon review of the vial, it is a multi-dose vial of lidocaine without epinephrine. Assuming this is, in fact, an allergic reaction to the injected medication, which of the following is the MOST LIKELY causal agent?
explanation: Overall, allergic reactions to local anesthetics are uncommon. Most untoward reactions to local anesthetics are non-allergic, and most patients who report allergies to local anesthetics are in fact not allergic when tested by skin testing. For example, a patient who recalls pounding in the chest when injected local anesthetic by their dentist is more likely to have had a physiologic (nonallergic) reaction to the epinephrine content of that formulation. In cases of true allergy, aminoester local anesthetics (procaine, chloroprocaine, etc) are more likely to elicit allergic reactions compared to aminoamides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, etc) because the aminoesters are derivatives of paraaminobenzoic acid (PABA), a known allergen (hapten to be precise). Although allergic reactions to aminoamides are very rare, patients may occasionally react to preservatives such as methylparaben contained in the aminoamide formulation. Multiple-dose vials of lidocaine typically contain 0.1% of methylparaben added as preservative, whereas single dose solutions are typically methylparaben free. Methylparaben is the methyl ester of para-hydroxybenzoic acid, which is structurally similar to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), differing only in having a hydroxyl group vs amino group in the para position. Thus, cross-sensitivity between these compounds can occur. Answers A & D: Aminoester local anesthetics are derivatives of paraaminobenzoic acid, which is known to be allergenic. Lidocaine is an amino-amide, not an amino-ester.
rationales: Sulfites such as sodium metabisulfite are added as antioxidants for the catecholamine content. Lidocaine vials with epinephrine will typically contain metabisulfite, which may also elicit allergic responses. This vial did not contain epinephrine.
bottomLine: True allergic reactions to local anesthetics are rare. Aminoester local anesthetics are more likely to elicit allergic reactions compared to aminoamides because they are derivatives of para-aminobenzoic acid, a known allergen. Also potential allergens are the preservatives included in some formulations, methylparaben (structurally related to PABA) and sulfites.

stem: Which of the following is a recognized side effect of methohexital?
explanation: Methohexital lowers the seizure threshold and may trigger seizures in susceptible patients. Methohexital is a short-acting barbiturate anesthetic. It binds to GABAA receptors which leads to neuronal hyperpolarization and inhibition of neurotransmission. Methohexital remains the drug of choice for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) because of longer seizure times (versus propofol), shorter awakening times (versus thiopental), and fewer side effects (versus etomidate). For ECT, methohexital is considered to cause no change in seizure duration overall. However, compared with saline it will decrease seizure duration during ECT. Methohexital is also commonly used as an induction agent for anesthesia for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) since, unlike many other IV anesthetics, it does not raise the seizure threshold and can increase ictal activity at low doses (e.g. 0.75 - 0.9 mg/kg). Administration of methohexital to patients with a history of seizures or epilepsy can trigger a new-onset seizure. However, methohexital has not been known to trigger a seizure in patients without any other risk factors. Similarly, there have been no reports of recurrent spontaneous seizures following methohexital administration for ECT. See the table below for other side effects of methohexital. Note that the excitatory side effects (e.g., hiccups, muscle twitches) are more prominent than those seen in most other IV anesthetics. The three commonly used barbiturates for induction of anesthesia are methohexital, thiopental, and thiamylal. However, methohexital is the only one commonly used in the United States. The complications of injecting barbiturates include a garlic or onion taste (40% of patients with thiopental or thiamylal), allergic reactions, local tissue irritation, and rarely tissue necrosis. The sulfur molecule in thiopental and thiamylal is the likely cause of the abnormal taste with induction, and the lack of this molecule explains why the abnormal taste is not seen with methohexital. Thiopental and thiamylal produce fewer excitatory symptoms with induction than methohexital, which produces cough, hiccough (hiccups), tremors, and twitching approximately five times more often. Hiccups with methohexital can be severe and cause distress for patients in the post-anesthesia recovery unit. Tissue irritation and local complications may occur more frequently with the use of thiopental and thiamylal than with methohexital. In comparative studies, pain on injection was shown to be greater with methohexital (12%) than with thiopental (9%). Results also show phlebitis occurs more frequently with methohexital use (8%) than with thiopental use (1%). Tissue and venous irritation are more common if a 5% solution is used, rather than the standard 2% solution. Answers A & B & C: Methohexital is not known to cause atrial fibrillation, diarrhea, or QT prolongation.
bottomLine: Unlike most other IV anesthetics, methohexital has epileptogenic activity and can induce seizures in at-risk patients. See the table above for other side effects of methohexital.
trueLearnInsight: Reconstituted vecuronium, which has an acidic pH, should not be mixed with alkaline solutions (e.g. barbiturate solutions such as methohexital) in the same syringe or administered simultaneously during intravenous infusion through the same needle or same intravenous line as they will precipitate and could occlude the intravenous line.

Brunton, Goodman and Gilman’s The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 12th edition, pp. 588-589. Mahisekar UL, et al. Infusion of large particles of thiopental sodium during anesthesia induction. J Clin Anesth. 1994 JanFeb;6(1):55-8.

stem: Which of the following is associated with ketamine?

options.text: Attenuation of respiratory response to carbon dioxide
options.html: Attenuation of respiratory response to carbon dioxide

options.text: Decreased cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen
options.html: Decreased cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen

explanation: Airway reflexes under ketamine anesthesia are maintained. Ketamine has been used frequently for procedural sedation in the emergency department. Airway reflexes have been found to be maintained in multiple studies. Further, aspiration is unlikely even when used for procedural sedation in an unsecured airway. Quoted from a review on the topic, "Despite 30 years of widespread ketamine use, there are no documented cases of clinically significant ketamine-associated aspiration in a patient lacking established contraindications to this drug." That being said, there is significant controversy regarding whether these reflexes are "protective" or not. The general consensus is that airway reflexes are preserved but these should not be assumed to be protective. Ketamine maintains better airway protective reflexes than many other anesthetics, but they are dose related (higher doses means less protective airway reflexes). Although an induction dose will likely preserve reflexes in a non-fasted patient without issue, it is not 100% protective against aspiration in a non-fasted patient. Ketamine, even at low serum levels, can produce powerful analgesia. The mechanism includes mu opioid receptor agonism and NMDA receptor antagonism. At higher doses, ketamine can produce hallucinations, amnesia, and increased sympathetic tone.
rationales:
Ketamine produces “dissociative amnesia,” in which protective reflexes and respiratory drive are relatively preserved in comparison to a similar anesthetic depth with other intravenous anesthetic agents.
Answer B: Ketamine increases CMRO2.
Answer C: The predominant hemodynamic effect of ketamine is indirect myocardial stimulation. Some direct myocardial depression is seen, however this is almost never clinically significant due to the indirect stimulation effects, even in critically ill patients.
bottomLine: Ketamine is unique when compared to many other intravenous anesthetics: airway reflexes and respiratory drive are relatively preserved, significant analgesia is produced, and sympathetic tone is increased. Ketamine's analgesic effect is present even with relatively small doses.

stem: Extravasation of which of the following drugs is LEAST likely to cause local tissue injury?
explanation: Extravasated propofol is associated with minimal local tissue injury. Many IV medications administered perioperatively are considered irritants, meaning they cause pain and/or slight damage to local tissue when extravasated. This may be an effect of the medication itself, or more commonly, due to a solvent or preservative. Despite even small amounts of propofol causing substantial pain with intravascular injection or upon extravasation, it is an irritant associated with minimal local tissue injury. Medications are considered vesicants if they cause extensive tissue injury or destruction. Most commonly, these medications fall into one of several categories including chemotherapeutics, vasoactive substances, concentrated electrolyte solutions, and hyperosmolar solutions. Mechanisms of tissue injury include direct cytotoxic effects, severe vasoconstriction, and increased osmotic pressure leading to compartment syndrome and ischemia. Answers A & B & C & E: Diazepam, phenytoin, promethazine, and thiopental are vesicants. Extravasation of each of these medications has been associated with severe local tissue necrosis, gangrene, or amputation.
bottomLine: Multiple specific drugs or drug classes are associated with severe local tissue injury and necrosis if extravasation occurs. Care should be taken to administer these drugs through easily visible, reliable peripheral or central intravenous access.

Extravasation injury of the upper extremity by intravenous phenytoin. Anesth Analg 2002; 94(3): 672-673. Schummer W, et al. Extravasation injury in the perioperative setting. Anesth Analg 2005; 100(3): 722-727.

stem: Which of the following is MOST commonly seen with the use of ketorolac?

options.text: Increased PT/INR with concomitant warfarin therapy
options.html: Increased PT/INR with concomitant warfarin therapy

options.text: Inhibition of afferent renal artery vasodilatation
options.html: Inhibition of afferent renal artery vasodilatation

options.text: Inhibition of efferent renal artery vasoconstriction
options.html: Inhibition of efferent renal artery vasoconstriction

explanation: Ketorolac inhibits afferent renal artery vasodilation. Ketorolac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). Ketorolac inhibits cyclooxygenase and prevents the formation of prostaglandins and thromboxane. Prostaglandins have protective effects on the gastrointestinal and renal systems. Thromboxane is produced by platelets and increases platelet activation. NSAIDs, therefore, have reversible anti-platelet activity. Prostaglandins cause vasodilatation of the afferent renal artery, increasing renal blood flow. Inhibition of prostaglandins will therefore prevent the increase in renal blood flow. For short-duration therapy, ketorolac has not been shown to affect renal function to any clinical significance. However, after 5 days of maximal therapy, ketorolac has been associated with renal dysfunction. This is a result of the prostaglandin inhibition of ketorolac resulting in decreased renal blood flow.
rationales:
Ketorolac has anti-platelet effects, which can increase the incidence of bleeding when co-administered with warfarin. Ketorolac does not affect the prothrombin time (PT)/international normalized ratio (INR). Ketorolac also has no effect on the free fraction of warfarin in the bloodstream. Warfarin is highly protein bound, so any drug that displaces it from albumin will effectively increase the potency of warfarin with a subsequent increase in INR.
Answer C: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors will inhibit efferent renal artery vasoconstriction, which can lead to renal dysfunction in the proper setting.
bottomLine: Ketorolac can decrease the glomerular filtration rate, especially when administered for greater than 5 days, via inhibition of afferent renal artery vasodilation.

stem: Chloroprocaine’s rapid onset of action is secondary to what characteristic of the drug?
explanation: Chloroprocaine (2-chloroprocaine) has a very fast onset of action because it is used in relatively high concentrations (eg, 3%) compared to other local anesthetics. 2-Chloroprocaine is a local anesthetic that blocks electrical conductivity in neurons by blocking the sodium channels. It is an ester-type local anesthetic and, just as other esters, is broken down by plasma cholinesterases. The amide local anesthetics undergo hepatic metabolism. 2-Chloroprocaine is the most rapidly metabolized of all of the local anesthetics, having a plasma half-life of 12 seconds in adults. The onset time of all local anesthetics is dependent on many factors, including lipid solubility, pKa, concentration, and injection site. It has been frequently stated that the onset time of a local anesthetic is correlated to the pKa. Only the nonionized base penetrates the nerve cell membrane and has a physiologic effect. The pKa of a local anesthetic is the pH at which the fraction of ionized and nonionized drug is equal. stem: For which of the following operations is the use of nitrous oxide MOST appropriate?

options.text: Exploratory laparotomy for small bowel obstruction with extensive lysis of adhesions
options.html: Exploratory laparotomy for small bowel obstruction with extensive lysis of adhesions

options.text: Open total colectomy for an obstructing tumor
options.html: Open total colectomy for an obstructing tumor

explanation: Nitrous oxide is not contraindicated for short abdominal operations such as a laparoscopic cholecystectomy or appendectomy. One study found that nitrous oxide had no clinically apparent deleterious effects during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Another study found that nitrous oxide did not cause noticeable bowel distention during laparoscopic bariatric procedures of relatively short duration. The amount of time using nitrous oxide during abdominal surgery is more important than the type of surgery being performed. Nitrous oxide is greater than 30 times more soluble in blood than nitrogen, so it readily diffuses into gaseous areas of the body, such as the gut, faster than nitrogen can diffuse out. Increasing the length of time that nitrous oxide is administered and the concentration at which it is delivered contributes to increasing bowel distention. There is a linear relationship with time administered to increase in bowel distension with up to a 200% increases in volume after 4 hours. A 50% concentration of nitrous oxide can double bowel gas, a 75% concentration can quadruple the volume, whereas an 80% mixture can lead to a fivefold increase after several hours of administration. It is worth noting that at 75% nitrous oxide there may be a much more rapid increase in volume when referring to a pneumothorax. Pneumothorax may double in volume by 10 minutes and may triple it by 30 minutes. Equilibration and volume increase may occur within seconds in the case of air embolism.
rationales:
Because of its ability to distend bowel, nitrous oxide is normally avoided in situations where the bowel is already distended or during long abdominal operations since it can lead to ischemia and poor operating conditions. A patient with adhesions leading to small bowel obstruction would likely already have inflamed, distended bowel and may require a lengthy operation.
Answer C: Nitrous oxide is not recommended for laparoscopic donor nephrectomy since bowel distention can lead to poor surgical visualization. In one study, nitrous oxide had to be discontinued in 1/4th of these because the surgical team could not continue with the operation secondary to bowel distention.
Answer D: Whether the operation is accomplished laparoscopically or via laparotomy does not, in itself, determine the appropriateness of nitrous oxide use. Rather, the length of the operation and presence of obstruction, cancer, or diverticulitis, for example, lead to preexisting bowel distention that nitrous oxide has the potential to exacerbate.
bottomLine: Nitrous oxide should be avoided in situations where bowel distention could be particularly hazardous. Both the length of time administered and the concentration of nitrous oxide lead to increasing bowel distention.
trueLearnInsight: An air-filled endotracheal tube cuff is susceptible to expansion by nitrous oxide. At 75% nitrous oxide a cuff can double or triple in volume causing pressure on the tracheal mucosa. Similarly, nitrous oxide may expand the cuffs of balloon-tipped (e.g. pulmonary artery) catheters. The air expansion is rapid and a doubling of catheter volume may occur within 10 minutes.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the potency of isoflurane is TRUE?

options.text: Isoflurane has a lower blood-gas partition coefficient than desflurane
options.html: Isoflurane has a lower blood-gas partition coefficient than desflurane

options.text: Isoflurane is more lipid soluble than sevoflurane
options.html: Isoflurane is more lipid soluble than sevoflurane

options.text: Isoflurane is the least potent of all the volatile anesthetics
options.html: Isoflurane is the least potent of all the volatile anesthetics

options.text: The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of isoflurane is approximately 1.8%
options.html: The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of isoflurane is approximately 1.8%

explanation: Isoflurane is the most lipid soluble of the three commonly used volatile anesthetics in the United States (desflurane, sevoflurane, and isoflurane) and is also the most potent of the three. There is a correlation between lipid solubility, or oil:gas partition coefficient, and potency of volatile anesthetic agents. This was first discovered by Meyer and Overton in the early 1900s and termed the Meyer-Overton correlation. The Meyer-Overton correlation attempted to explain the mechanism of action of volatile anesthetics which has been proven to be overly simplistic; however, the fact that there is a correlation between lipid solubility and potency of the common volatile agents remains true.
rationales:
The blood-gas partition coefficient of inhalational anesthetics correlates with the speed of onset and offset, not the potency. Isoflurane has the highest blood-gas partition coefficient of desflurane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane. The order of bloodgas partition coefficient is isoflurane >> sevoflurane > desflurane, which is also inversely proportional to their speed of onset and offset, desflurane > sevoflurane >> isoflurane.
Answer C: Isoflurane is more potent than sevoflurane and desflurane. Nitrous oxide is even less potent than desflurane with a MAC of >100%; however, it is technically an inhalational anesthetic and not a volatile anesthetic as it is a gas at standard ambient conditions compared to the volatile anesthetics which are volatile liquids under the same ambient conditions. Of note, halothane is even more potent than isoflurane and although not used in the United States, is still used throughout the world.
Answer D: The MAC is a measure of potency of an inhaled anesthetic, with a lower number indicating a lower percentage of partial pressure of the agent needed to prevent movement to a surgical stimulus in 50% of the population. The MAC of isoflurane is generally cited around 1.1%, while the MAC of sevoflurane is usually cited around 1.8% (1.7%-2.2%). The MAC of desflurane is approximately 6.6%
bottomLine: Isoflurane is a potent volatile anesthetic with a MAC near 1.1%. In terms of inhalational anesthetic potency, isoflurane (MAC ~1%) > sevoflurane (MAC ~2%) >> desflurane (MAC ~6%) >>> nitrous oxide (MAC ~104%).
trueLearnInsight: The Tec 9 Datex-Ohmeda vaporizer heats desflurane to 2 atmospheres in order to ensure reliability of the dialed concentration. This is because desflurane is near boiling point at room temperature, which means an unpredictable amount is in liquid form, while the rest of it may be in gaseous form. This heated vaporizer reliably converts desflurane to the gaseous form.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Volatile Anesthetic: Isoflurane Potency" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 414, 423. Miller, Basics of Anesthesia, 7th edition, Inhalational Anesthetics. Gropper. Miller's Anesthesia. 9th Edition. Inhaled Anesthetics: Mechanisms of Action.

stem: Which of the following MOST closely approximates the time for onset of action of 2-chloroprocaine administered via epidural catheter?
explanation: Epidural 2-chloroprocaine has an onset time of approximately 6-12 minutes, as a result of the high concentration of local anesthetic that is used. The ester local anesthetic 2-chloroprocaine is most frequently used in the setting of obstetric epidural analgesia. Compared to other commonly used local anesthetics, is has the fastest onset of action time. 2-chloroprocaine has an onset time of 6-12 minutes, and that may be shortened slightly when high volumes are used. It is available in a 2% and 3% concentration. Duration of action is 45-60 minutes plain and 60-90 minutes when mixed with epinephrine (1:200,000 dilution). Chloroprocaine is hydrolyzed rapidly by plasma cholinesterases (half-life elimination of 21 seconds). However, metabolism is decreased in patients with a pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Chloroprocaine is commonly used to obtain rapid analgesia for an emergency cesarean section, when a working epidural catheter is already in place. Answers A & C: The onset of action for chloroprocaine via the epidural route is 6-12 minutes.
bottomLine: Chloroprocaine has the fastest onset of action time among commonly used epidural local anesthetics at 6-12 minutes. It has the shortest duration of action of all the local anesthetics.
trueLearnInsight: Administration of 2-chloroprocaine may decrease the efficacy of subsequently administered neuraxial drugs including bupivacaine, morphine, and fentanyl. Chloroaminobenzoic acid (the metabolite of 2-chloroprocaine) may be responsible for decreasing the efficacy of subsequent bupivacaine administration. Chloroaminobenzoic acid may also act as an antagonist of the µ-opioid receptor, leading to reduced efficacy of subsequent opioid neuraxial administration.

stem: Which of the following is the MOST LIKELY explanation for increased hydrocodone requirements in a patient with a history of chronic pain who has just started fluoxetine for the treatment of fibromyalgia?
explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), specifically fluoxetine and paroxetine, significantly inhibit CYP2D6 and slow the conversion of hydrocodone to hydromorphone within the liver. While oral hydrocodone itself has an analgesic potency that is comparable to morphine when it is administered orally, its metabolite hydromorphone has roughly 4 times greater analgesic efficacy. Inhibition of the CYP2D6 enzyme may, therefore, result in less clinical analgesic effect than otherwise might be gained from the ingestion of hydrocodone. Codeine, hydrocodone, and oxycodone are all medications converted by the cytochrome P450 system (specifically CYP2D6) into metabolites with greater analgesic potency (morphine, hydromorphone, and oxymorphone respectively). It should be noted that codeine itself is a prodrug and has minimal to no intrinsic analgesic properties and only exerts its clinical effect through these conversions. Both hydrocodone and oxycodone have similar intrinsic analgesic properties to morphine, with hydrocodone tending to be a slightly weaker analgesic and oxycodone tending to be slightly stronger than morphine itself. The conversion of hydrocodone to hydromorphone increases its analgesic potency by a factor of 4, and the conversion of oxycodone to oxymorphone increases its analgesic potency by a factor of 2. Drug interactions involving the cytochrome P450 isoforms generally result from one of two processes: enzyme inhibition or enzyme induction. The CYP2D6 enzyme is responsible for the metabolism of many psychotherapeutic agents. Inactive forms of this enzyme can increase requirements for opioid prodrugs since conversion to the active forms is significantly reduced. For example, 7-10% of Caucasians express an inactive homozygous form of CYP2D6, which does not facilitate the O-methylation of codeine into morphine, producing a minimal clinical effect from the ingestion of this drug. Conversely, a small proportion of the population possesses a CYP2D6 phenotype that causes rapid metabolism of this same drug, resulting in potentially dangerous clinical levels of morphine following the ingestion of a routine dose of codeine. It is for this reason that codeine is has received a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warning for its use in pediatric patients undergoing tonsillectomy.
rationales:
Hydrocodone is not significantly metabolized by CYP3A4 or CYP1A2.
Answer C: Tolerance is the state in which increased doses of the same substance are needed to achieve the desired effect. In this question, the acute rise in drug consumption following the initiation of a drug that has been shown to improve symptoms of their pain syndrome should alert the clinician to a possibly undesirable drug interaction.
bottomLine: SSRIs inhibit CYP2D6 which reduces the activation of many opioids (e.g. codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone) to more potent forms (eg, morphine, hydromorphone, oxymorphone).

Drug Alcohol Depend. 2008;98(3):191–202.

stem: Which of the following is a N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist?
explanation: Nitrous oxide is a mixed competitive/noncompetitive antagonist at the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA) receptor. Although nitrous oxide interacts at multiple receptor types (including, but not limited to, glycine, nicotinic acetylcholine, and serotonin receptors), it is via its NMDA antagonism that most of its anesthetic effects are thought to be mediated. The NMDA receptor is a class of glutamate-activated ion channels that conducts sodium, potassium, and calcium ions. It is involved in the long-term modulation of synaptic responses and is associated with synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. Activation of the receptor increases the intracellular concentration of calcium that then functions as a second messenger via multiple pathways. Activation also results in sodium influx and potassium efflux. Some examples of drugs that act on the NMDA receptor: • Dextromethorphan is an over-the-counter cough suppressant with NMDA antagonist properties. It can be abused recreationally in large doses because it acts as a dissociative anesthetic. • Ketamine is a potent, selective NMDA inhibitor that binds to the phencyclidine site on the receptor. Antagonism results in (dissociative) anesthesia, analgesia, amnesia, bronchodilation, and maintenance of protective airway reflexes. Side effects include hallucinations or other psychomimetic reactions (improved or prevented with benzodiazepines or propofol), salivation (improved or prevented with antisialagogues such as glycopyrrolate), and increases in intraocular pressure, intracranial pressure, and cerebral metabolic rate. • Magnesium has NMDA antagonist activity. Physiologically, it blocks the NMDA ion channel at resting membrane potential. Depolarization must occur to remove the magnesium and allow calcium, sodium, and potassium to cross the ion channel. • Phencyclidine, also known as angel dust, is a dissociative drug that acts via NMDA antagonism with no known medical use. It is abused as a recreational drug, and patients may present after intoxication. These patients may be agitated, be violent, and have nystagmus. Despite agitation and possible violence, they likely have reduced minimum alveolar concentration requirements. • Nonhalogenated inhalational anesthetics (eg, nitrous oxide and xenon) are thought to act primarily through NMDA antagonism. Halogenated volatile anesthetics (eg, sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane) result in NMDA antagonism at very high doses, but this is not thought to be of significant clinical importance.
rationales:
Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that does not have any effects at the NMDA receptor. Opioids that do exhibit some NMDA antagonism include propoxyphene (no longer available in the United States), methadone, and tramadol.
Answer C: Propofol is a γ-aminobutyric acid agonist, not an NMDA antagonist.
bottomLine: Multiple medications commonly used perioperatively function as N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonists. Examples include but are not limited to ketamine, magnesium sulfate, nitrous oxide, and certain opioids including methadone and tramadol.

explanationHtml:
Nitrous oxide is a mixed competitive/noncompetitive antagonist at the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA) receptor.

Although nitrous oxide interacts at multiple receptor types (including, but not limited to, glycine, nicotinic acetylcholine, and serotonin receptors), it is via its NMDA antagonism that most of its anesthetic effects are thought to be mediated.

The NMDA receptor is a class of glutamate-activated ion channels that conducts sodium, potassium, and calcium ions. It is involved in the long-term modulation of synaptic responses and is associated with synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory.

Activation of the receptor increases the intracellular concentration of calcium that then functions as a second messenger via multiple pathways. Activation also results in sodium influx and potassium efflux.

Some examples of drugs that act on the NMDA receptor:

  • Dextromethorphan is an over-the-counter cough suppressant with NMDA antagonist properties. It can be abused recreationally in large doses because it acts as a dissociative anesthetic.
  • Ketamine is a potent, selective NMDA inhibitor that binds to the phencyclidine site on the receptor. Antagonism results in (dissociative) anesthesia, analgesia, amnesia, bronchodilation, and maintenance of protective airway reflexes. Side effects include hallucinations or other psychomimetic reactions (improved or prevented with benzodiazepines or propofol), salivation (improved or prevented with antisialagogues such as glycopyrrolate), and increases in intraocular pressure, intracranial pressure, and cerebral metabolic rate.
  • Magnesium has NMDA antagonist activity. Physiologically, it blocks the NMDA ion channel at resting membrane potential. Depolarization must occur to remove the magnesium and allow calcium, sodium, and potassium to cross the ion channel.
  • Phencyclidine, also known as angel dust, is a dissociative drug that acts via NMDA antagonism with no known medical use. It is abused as a recreational drug, and patients may present after intoxication. These patients may be agitated, be violent, and have nystagmus. Despite agitation and possible violence, they likely have reduced minimum alveolar concentration requirements.
  • Nonhalogenated inhalational anesthetics (eg, nitrous oxide and xenon) are thought to act primarily through NMDA antagonism. Halogenated volatile anesthetics (eg, sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane) result in NMDA antagonism at very high doses, but this is not thought to be of significant clinical importance.

• Answer A: Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that does not have any effects at the NMDA receptor. Opioids that do exhibit some NMDA antagonism include propoxyphene (no longer available in the United States), methadone, and tramadol.
  • Answer C: Propofol is a γ-aminobutyric acid agonist, not an NMDA antagonist.

stem: A 3-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with shortness of breath. Chest radiograph shows an object lodged in the right mainstem bronchus. The patient is taken to the operating room for removal of the foreign body. Which of the following is MOST accurate regarding induction of anesthesia in this patient compared to a healthy child?

options.text: Inhalational induction with isoflurane will be faster
options.html: Inhalational induction with isoflurane will be faster

options.text: Intravenous induction will have a faster onset
options.html: Intravenous induction will have a faster onset

options.text: The rate of rise in FA/FI ratio for desflurane will decrease
options.html: The rate of rise in FA/FI ratio for desflurane will decrease

explanation: An object lodged in the right mainstem bronchus will prevent ventilation to a lung that is perfused, creating an intrapulmonary shunt. In the presence of a right-to-left shunt, inhalational induction will be slower. In other words, the rate of rise for the alveolar concentration to inspired concentration (FA/FI) of desflurane will decrease. A right to left shunt, both intrapulmonary and intracardiac, slow inhalational induction. This is due to the dilution of the anesthetic agent when venous blood that has bypassed the lungs mixes with arterial blood. This delay is more obvious with the less soluble agents, such as desflurane and nitrous oxide. Comparing the two, nitrous oxide will be more affected than desflurane due to the concentration effect. The concentration effect explains why the rate of rise of FA/FI is faster for nitrous oxide even though the blood-gas coefficient is lower for desflurane. Soluble agents such as isoflurane may see minimal or no delay in induction. Intravenous induction is mainly affected by right to left intracardiac shunts (eg, Eisenmenger syndrome) and results in faster induction since the lungs are bypassed. More common intracardiac shunts (eg, ventricular septal defect with left to right shunting) will have minimal effect on either IV or inhalational induction. An intrapulmonary shunt will not affect the speed of intravenous induction. The chart below shows a summary of the various shunts and how anesthetic agents are affected.
rationales:
A right to left shunt, both intrapulmonary and intracardiac, slow inhalation induction.
Answer B: An intrapulmonary shunt will not affect the speed of intravenous induction.
bottomLine: Right to left shunt slows the speed of inhalational induction. This is more obvious in less soluble agents. In the presence of an intrapulmonary shunt, the speed of induction will affect (most to least): Nitrous Oxide > Desflurane > Sevoflurane > Isoflurane > Halothane.
trueLearnInsight: Endobronchial intubation is another situation that produces a right to left intrapulmonary shunt.

stem: The pharmacy is reviewing the epidural infusate solution composition at a hospital and consults with the anesthesiologists. It is determined that a hydrophilic opioid with low lipophilicity is desired for the epidural infusate. Which of the following opioids has the LOWEST lipophilicity?
explanation: With an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 1.3, hydromorphone has the lowest lipophilicity of any of the listed opioids. All of the other opioids listed are considered lipophilic, while hydromorphone and morphine are considered hydrophilic. The physiological effects of intrathecal use of opioids depend on many factors, such as lipid solubility. Fentanyl and sufentanil, both highly lipid soluble, have a rapid onset and short duration compared to less lipid-soluble opioids such as morphine. Increased lipid solubility leads to increased uptake into neurons, blood vessels, and fatty tissue. The spread of opioids within the cerebrospinal fluid is more extensive with the less lipid-soluble (ie, hydrophilic) opioids, such as morphine, compared to the more lipid-soluble opioids. The spread is more extensive with the hydrophilic opioids due to the slower uptake into blood vessels and elimination from the cerebrospinal fluid and epidural space. Because hydrophilic opioids spread more extensively and persist longer within the cerebrospinal fluid or epidural space, they have a higher risk of respiratory depression after intrathecal injection hours after use. Approximate values of the octanol/H2O partition coefficient of various opioids
rationales:
Alfentanil has an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 145, making it more lipophilic.
Answer B: Fentanyl has an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 813, making it one of the most lipophilic.
Answer D: Sufentanil has an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 1778, making it the most lipophilic of the opioids listed.
bottomLine: When opioids are used for neuraxial anesthesia, hydrophilic opioids spread more extensively and persist longer within the cerebrospinal fluid or epidural space. The order of the least to the most lipophilic opioids based on the octanol/H2O partition coefficient is hydromorphone (1.3) > morphine (1.4) > alfentanil (145) > fentanyl (813) > and sufentanil (1778).

stem: Which of the following drugs exerts most of its beneficial effects via the kappa opioid receptor?
explanation: Meperidine has its effect upon the kappa (κ) opioid receptor. Meperidine use has become less common due to its wide side effect profile and long half-life of its active metabolites (14-21 hours). This becomes particularly important in renal failure patients where metabolites can accumulate, notably normeperidine, which is proconvulsant. Despite these limitations, meperidine is still used today primarily to treat shivering from multiple causes including general anesthesia, epidural anesthesia, fever, transfusion reactions, and following the administration of amphotericin B. Studies show that this anti-shivering effect occurs without affecting the mu (µ) opioid receptor, but rather is a multimodal effect that focuses upon the κ receptor. Meperidine does have analgesic properties (potency 1/10 that of morphine) mediated by both mu and κ receptors. The major subtypes of opioid receptors include µ, κ, and delta (δ). The µ receptor is responsible for the most commonly recognized properties of opioids and has three subclasses. The µ1 receptor produces the analgesic and physical dependence properties of most opioids while stimulation of the µ2 receptor results in respiratory depression, miosis, euphoria, decreased gastrointestinal motility, and physical dependence. The actions of µ3 receptors are unknown but may mediate some anti-inflammatory activity. The κ receptor mediates analgesia but also dysphoria, sedation, miosis, and inhibits antidiuretic hormone release. The δ receptor is responsible for analgesia, physical dependence, and perhaps antidepressant effects. Partial agonists and mixed agonist-antagonist agents, such as nalbuphine, have differential effects at each receptor site. Nalbuphine works as a kappaagonist/mu-antagonist analgesic.
rationales:
Methadone exerts significant effects on the mu opioid receptor. Methadone also acts on the NMDA receptor as an antagonist. NMDA receptor antagonism explains methadone's effect for neuropathic pain and in opioid tolerance. Methadone does prolong the QT interval and should be monitored.
Answer C: Morphine has its main effect on the mu opioid receptor. Morphine is metabolized by the liver to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G). More morphine is metabolized to M3G than M6G. However M6G is an active metabolite of morphine.
Answer D: Remifentanil has its main effect upon the mu opioid receptor. Remifentanil is unique with a very short half-life which is not affected by the infusion time. Remifentanil is metabolized by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases.
bottomLine: Meperidine’s beneficial effects are multimodal and center around the kappa opioid receptor.
trueLearnInsight: Meperidine has structural similarities to atropine. Which is why meperidine is the only opioid associated with increases in heart rate following administration. Meperidine also has some weak local anesthetic effects.

stem: Which of the following can be seen after administration of inhaled albuterol?
explanation: Tachycardia is the most common side effect associated with albuterol. Albuterol is the most common beta-agonist that is used perioperatively. Albuterol is selective for the beta-2 receptors and causes relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle. Albuterol can be used to treat bronchospasm, asthma, or wheezing, or it can be used prophylactically to reduce postoperative respiratory complications in high-risk patients (eg, recent respiratory infection, smoking, etc). Albuterol can be administered to the patient before the induction of anesthesia, intraoperatively through the endotracheal tube, or after extubation. The most common side effect of albuterol is tachycardia from the beta effect on the heart. Premature ventricular contractions are also commonly seen with albuterol use. Diastolic hypotension can be seen after large doses of albuterol. Central nervous system beta receptor stimulation from albuterol can lead to agitation and tremors. Beta-agonists also cause a decrease in potassium, which can result in hypokalemia because beta-adrenergic agonists cause potassium to shift intracellularly.
rationales:
Burst suppression pattern on electroencephalography (EEG) tracing is seen because the depth of anesthesia is increased after volatile or intravenous anesthetic use. This burst suppression pattern is initially observed at bispectral index scale values between the range of 20 and 40. Albuterol has not been shown to alter EEG results.
Answer B: Albuterol and beta-adrenergic agonists are associated with hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, due to the intracellular shift of potassium.
Answer C: Diastolic hypotension, not hypertension, can be seen after albuterol use.
bottomLine: Tachycardia is the most commonly observed side effect of inhaled albuterol. Beta-adrenergic drugs, such as albuterol, can also cause hypokalemia due to the intracellular shift of potassium.

stem: Which of the following statements about patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency is TRUE?

options.text: The K-variant is the least common pseudocholinesterase gene variant
options.html: The K-variant is the least common pseudocholinesterase gene variant

options.text: Succinylcholine duration of action is shortened
options.html: Succinylcholine duration of action is shortened

options.text: Mivacurium duration of action is prolonged
options.html: Mivacurium duration of action is prolonged

explanation: Mivacurium is metabolized by butyrylcholinesterase (BCHE) and therefore its effect is prolonged in patients with BCHE deficiency. Butyrylcholinesterase (alternately pseudocholinesterase or plasma cholinesterase) is the enzyme responsible for degradation of succinylcholine and mivacurium. Administration of either of these medications to patients with BCHE deficiency therefore results in prolonged neuromuscular blockade and the potential for prolonged apnea. Butyrylcholinesterase deficiency is an inherited trait that may be homozygous or heterozygous. The incidence of the heterozygous atypical type is approximately 1:500. Individuals with this genotype may experience an increase in duration of effect of succinylcholine by 50-100% (typically 20-30 minutes). The incidence of homozygous atypical is 1:3000, and this causes an increase in duration of effect by 4-8 hours. Approximately 20 genetic variants of the BCHE gene exist with the A- and K-variants being the most common.
rationales:
The A and K variants are the most common.
Answer B: Duration of action is prolonged.
bottomLine: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency prolongs the duration of action of succinylcholine and mivacurium, which can lead to prolonged neuromuscular blockade and apnea.
trueLearnInsight: Echothiophate is an anticholinesterase used to treat refractory glaucoma by causing miosis. Since it inhibits BCHE, systemic absorption can cause up to a 95% decrease in BCHE function, thereby potentiating the effects of succinylcholine.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Butyrylcholinesterase Deficiency" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 127, 511.

stem: Which of the following hemodynamic effects is MOST LIKELY to be seen immediately following 0.5 g/kg administration of mannitol given intravenously over twenty minutes?
explanation: After administration of mannitol, an increase in plasma volume will occur which will result in an increase in blood pressure and cardiac output. This may lead to an increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, especially in patients with heart failure. This increase may lead to pulmonary edema in certain patients. The term diuretic typically is applied to a medication that can decrease the extracellular fluid volume by increasing urinary water or solute excretion. Mannitol produces diuresis by increasing osmotic pressure in the proximal tubule and loop of Henle, causing a decrease in passive reabsorption of water and thus an increase in renal blood flow. Following the administration of mannitol, the excretion of sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, and chloride is increased. In the interstitial space, the increased osmotic pressure draws water from the cells to increase extracellular fluid which will further increase total plasma flow. There is a decrease in hematocrit and blood viscosity secondary to the hemodilution that occurs from solute extraction. An increase in blood pressure may also be seen depending on the systemic vascular resistance. stem: Which of the following medications causes the LEAST reduction in minimum alveolar concentration of volatile anesthetics?
explanation: Nalbuphine, a mixed opioid agonist-antagonist, lowers the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of volatile anesthetics by less than 10%, even at high doses (C). Unlike volatile anesthetics and certain IV anesthetics such as propofol, opioids have ceiling effects that prevent them from being used safely as sole anesthetic agents. This is evidenced by reports of recall and awareness in cases using high-dose fentanyl and even combinations of opioids and nitrous oxide. Administration of opioids with volatile anesthetics can significantly decrease the MAC. Still, there is a sub-MAC ceiling effect at which there is no further reduction in MAC despite increases in dose. This is further evidenced by monitoring the effects of opioid administration using EEG. Progressive changes are initially seen on EEG with increasing doses of opioids, but eventually, a ceiling effect occurs, and no further EEG changes are observed. By contrast, increasing concentrations of volatile anesthetics result in progressive EEG changes, ultimately inducing burst suppression and then an isoelectric EEG. Fentanyl and remifentanil (at equipotent doses) are very effective at lowering MAC, with up to an approximately 80% reduction observed at higher (but still clinically relevant) doses. Morphine can lower volatile anesthetic MAC by approximately 20-60%, depending on the dose. Partial opioid agonists and mixed agonist-antagonist agents, such as nalbuphine and butorphanol, do not have nearly as significant an effect on lowering MAC as pure opioid agonists. For example, despite having an analgesic potency nearly equivalent to morphine, nalbuphine lowers MAC by no more than 10%, even at high doses. Butorphanol lowers MAC only slightly more than 10%.
rationales:
Morphine can lower volatile anesthetic MAC by approximately 20-60%, depending on the dose.
Answer C: Fentanyl and remifentanil (at equipotent doses) are very effective at lowering MAC, with up to an approximately 80% reduction observed at higher (but still clinically relevant) doses.
bottomLine: Most opioids significantly lower volatile anesthetic MAC requirements when administered concurrently. However, partial opioid agonists and mixed agonist-antagonists have a greatly reduced, and nearly clinically insignificant, effect on MAC.

stem: Which of the following best describes the meaning of the ED95 dose in reference to neuromuscular blockers?

options.text: Dose of drug needed to achieve 95% blockade of receptors
options.html: Dose of drug needed to achieve 95% blockade of receptors

options.text: Dose of drug needed to achieve 50% single twitch depression in 95% of the population
options.html: Dose of drug needed to achieve 50% single twitch depression in 95% of the population

options.text: Dose of drug needed to achieve 95% twitch depression in 50% of the population
options.html: Dose of drug needed to achieve 95% twitch depression in 50% of the population

explanation: The ED95 of a neuromuscular blocking drug is the effective dose required to achieve 95% block of a single twitch in 50% of individuals. In general pharmacology, ED95 refers to the effective dose needed to get the desired effect for 95% of the population. Unfortunately, this term has a different meaning specifically for neuromuscular blocking agents. For these agents, ED95 refers to the median dose required to achieve a 95% reduction in the maximal twitch response from baseline, in 50% of the population. A more appropriate term would be ED5095, however the terminology ED95 has stuck for this context. The ED95 for rocuronium is 0.3 mg/kg, which means that half of patients will achieve at least a 95% blockade of a single twitch if they receive this weight-based dose. For effective relaxation during intubation, one to two times the ED95 is typically needed. This is why most practitioners use, for example, at least 0.6 mg/kg of rocuronium for intubation. The rapid sequence intubation dose of rocuronium is therefore four times ED95 (1.2 mg/kg). Dose response curves are used to determine potency of neuromuscular blocking agents. The relationship is plotted between twitch depression and weight-based dose. The ED95 is the median dose corresponding to a 95% single twitch depression. ED95 doses are used to compare potency between drugs. For example, the ED95 for vecuronium is 0.05 mg/kg and the intubating dose is 0.1 mg/kg. This indicates that vecuronium has a potency 6 times that of rocuronium. Therefore, six times the dose of rocuronium should be administered to achieve the same effect as vecuronium (i.e. 6 x 0.05 mg/kg = 0.3 mg/kg). Answers A & B: This is an incorrect description of the meaning of an ED95 dose.
bottomLine: ED95 is the effective dose of a neuromuscular blocking drug required to achieve 95% block of a single twitch in 50% of individuals who receive this drug and dose. For effective relaxation during intubation, one to two times the ED95 is typically administered.

stem: Why does the alveolar concentration (FA)/ inspired concentration (FI) curve rise faster for nitrous oxide compared to desflurane?
explanation: The rate of rise of the alveolar concentration (FA)/ inspired concentration (FI) ratio is more rapid for nitrous oxide compared to desflurane because of the concentration effect, despite nitrous oxide having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient (0.47) than desflurane (0.45). In general, the blood/gas solubility, measured as the blood/gas partition coefficient, is what determines the speed of onset and rate of rise of FA/FI with the lower the blood/gas partition coefficient, the faster the onset and rate of rise of FA/FI. However, nitrous oxide has the fastest rate of rise of any of the inhalational anesthetics despite having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient than desflurane. The reason that nitrous oxide has a faster onset of action than desflurane is due to the concentration effect. At equiamnestic inspired concentrations, the percentage of inspired nitrous oxide is far higher than that of desflurane. As the relatively large concentration (and therefore volume) of nitrous oxide is absorbed at the level of the alveoli, the remaining gas occupies a smaller volume. Therefore, mixed inspired gas from the conducting airways will replace this volume. This gas has the same high concentration of nitrous oxide, so this effect is perpetuated. In this way, ventilation is augmented above the minute ventilation. This makes a greater quantity of agents available to the lung for absorption for a given time period. This image illustrates the concentration-effect during a single inhalation. Much more nitrous oxide is absorbed than what would be expected as the concentration-effect draws more nitrous oxide into the alveoli from the conducting airways as large volumes of nitrous oxide already in the alveoli are absorbed. Illustration © TrueLearn, LLC
rationales:
Nitrous oxide exists as a gas at standard temperature and pressure, so vapor pressure is not relevant in this comparison.
Answer C: Nitrous oxide has a higher (0.47) blood/gas partition coefficient than desflurane (0.45).
Answer D: The second gas effect describes why the FA/FI ratio of a second anesthetic equilibrates more rapidly when nitrous oxide is used. This effect is not relevant when the rate of uptake of desflurane is compared to the rate of rise of nitrous oxide.
bottomLine: The absorption of nitrous oxide is augmented by the concentration effect, making the rate of absorption faster than that of desflurane despite having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Concentration Effect (B)" Gropper M, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Chapter 20: Inhaled Anesthetic Pharmacokinetics: Uptake, Distribution, Metabolism and Toxicity. 9th Edition.

stem: Which of the following would result in the biggest decrease in minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) in a 35-year-old adult patient who is undergoing anesthesia for a laparoscopic appendectomy with a volatile anesthetic?

options.text: Administration of 1 mg/kg of intravenous lidocaine
options.html: Administration of 1 mg/kg of intravenous lidocaine

options.text: Administration of 3 mcg/kg of intravenous fentanyl
options.html: Administration of 3 mcg/kg of intravenous fentanyl

options.text: Administration of oral gabapentin prior to induction of anesthesia
options.html: Administration of oral gabapentin prior to induction of anesthesia

explanation: Of all the answer choices, intravenous fentanyl would cause the largest decrease in MAC values. It has been shown that fentanyl will decrease MAC by 50% when 3 mcg/kg is used and up to 80% when 10 mcg/kg is used. Alfentanil, sufentanil, and remifentanil also possess the capability to decrease MAC. Anesthesia often consists of multiple agents that act synergistically to improve surgical conditions. Opioids are often added to volatile anesthetics to smooth the course and decrease the amount of volatile required. Often the combination of an opioid and volatile anesthetic is better tolerated hemodynamically than a volatile used alone. Animal data have shown that a significant reduction in MAC occurs with administration of opioids. The synthetic opioids (fentanyl, remifentanil, alfentanil, and sufentanil) result in a more significant decrease when compared with morphine and hydromorphone. Opioid partial agonists (nalbuphine and butorphanol) produce an even smaller reduction in MAC. Two studies indicate that “MAC awake” is much less affected by opioids than standard MAC. Factors that increase MAC: drugs (amphetamines, cocaine, ephedrine, chronic ethanol use), electrolytes (hypernatremia), and hyperthermia. Factors that decrease MAC: drugs (propofol, etomidate, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, ketamine, alpha-2-agonists, acute ethanol intoxication, local anesthetics, opioids, chronic amphetamine use, lithium, verapamil), elderly age, electrolytes (hyponatremia), anemia, hypercarbia, hypothermia, hypoxemia, and pregnancy (controversial).
rationales:
Intravenous lidocaine does decrease MAC in humans, however intravenous fentanyl would cause a larger decrease. In animal studies 1.5 mg/kg of lidocaine has been shown to decrease MAC by 10% to 30%.
Answer C: Gabapentin has not been shown to alter MAC values.
bottomLine: Intravenous opioids result in a decreased minimum alveolar concentration (MAC). The synthetic opioids cause a higher reduction in MAC compared to morphine. Gabapentin has not been shown to alter MAC values.

stem: A 26-year-old primigravida with a history of severe gastroesophageal reflux is scheduled to undergo an elective Cesarean section. The plan is to give her an oral histamine-2 receptor antagonist blocker prior to the surgery. Which of the following is the onset of action for oral famotidine?
explanation: Oral famotidine has an onset time of action of ~1 hr, while intravenous famotidine has an onset time of ~30 minutes. Parietal cells in the stomach have histamine-2 (H2) receptors and respond to histamine by secreting acid. Histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2 blockers), such as cimetidine and famotidine, can be used to reduce gastric acid secretion by blocking the effect of histamine on these receptors. Histamine-2 receptor blockers are occasionally used in the perioperative period to prevent sequelae from aspiration in high-risk patients. Recommendations for elective Cesarean section include pharmacologic prophylaxis for aspiration with a nonparticulate antacid, H2 blocker, metoclopramide, and/or a proton pump inhibitor in all patients because of the elevated risk of aspiration associated with pregnancy. The onset of action of the clinically used H2 blockers (primarily famotidine and cimetidine) are very similar, and they are typically given (IV or oral) 30 to 90 min before surgery. The duration of action of famotidine is longer (~10-12 hr) than that of cimetidine (~4-5 hr), independent of the route of administration. Cimetidine is associated with more adverse effects compared with famotidine, including the inhibition of the hepatic mixedfunction oxidase system prolonging the half-lives of drugs metabolized by this system, such as lidocaine, propranolol, and diazepam. Other side effects of chronic cimetidine use include gynecomastia and galactorrhea.
rationales:
Antacids have a near-immediate onset, with the peak effect seen within 15 to 30 min of oral administration. Antacids work by neutralizing acid in the stomach. Sodium citrate is the most common nonparticulate antacid used in Cesarean deliveries.
Answer B: The onset of IV famotidine is ~30 min. The onset is ~60 min via the oral route.
Answer D: The onset of proton pump inhibitors (PPI) is 1 to 3 hr when administered orally, but peak response may take up to 5 days. Proton pump inhibitors act by binding to hydrogen-potassium ATPases in the stomach and cause a permanent inhibition. Synthesis of new pumps takes about 24 hr, which explains the duration of action of PPIs.
bottomLine: The onset of action of the clinically used histamine-2 receptor blockers (primarily famotidine and cimetidine) are ~30 min (IV) and ~60 min (oral). The duration of action of famotidine is longer (~10-12 hr) than that of cimetidine (~4-5 hr), independent of the route of administration.
trueLearnInsight: In 2011, the American Society of Anesthesiologists task force found insufficient evidence to support the effect of administering histamine-2 receptor blockers (or other drugs such as proton pump inhibitors, antacids, antiemetics, and gastrokinetic agents) in the perioperative period on the incidence of pulmonary aspiration, emesis, or reflex; thus, they do not recommend their use in patients who do not have an increased risk of aspiration.
