stem: Which of the following opioid context-sensitive half-time curves represents alfentanil?
explanation: Curve B (purple) represents alfentanil. Context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. “Context” refers to the length of an infusion. For most drugs, the longer the infusion runs, the longer it takes for the drug plasma concentration to decline by half after the infusion is stopped. The CSHT reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drug plasma clearance is the collection of processes (e.g., metabolism, excretion, biotransformation, etc.) that remove the drug from plasma and therefore decrease the drug plasma concentration. If all other factors are identical, a drug with a high plasma clearance will have a lower CSHT than a drug with a low plasma clearance. When an infusion of a drug is running, a portion of the drug moves or redistributes down its concentration gradient from the central (plasma) compartment into peripheral (tissue) compartments. Once the drug infusion stops, the plasma concentration will decrease and the concentration gradient reverses. Then, the drug that has accumulated peripherally redistributes back into plasma. A drug with a slower redistribution back to plasma will have a faster CSHT than an otherwise identical drug with a faster redistribution. This occurs because the drug is being cleared from the plasma faster than the drug is returning from the periphery, and thus the plasma concentration falls faster. Keep in mind that CSHTs are different from elimination half-lives since the latter are the result of metabolism and excretion from the whole body, not just plasma. The time to decrease the plasma concentration by half (CSHT) is NOT related to the time to eliminate half of the drug from the body (“terminal half-life”). Propofol (blue line) has a steadily rising though relatively short CSHT even with a long duration of infusion. Due to its lipophilicity, propofol has a very large volume of distribution (150-700 L) and readily redistributes from the central compartment to the periphery during an infusion. This contributes to a somewhat long elimination half-life of six hours. However, the CSHT of propofol is relatively short since the drug has a high metabolic clearance from plasma (1500-2200 L/min) and a slow redistribution from peripheral to central. Fentanyl (green line), like propofol, is highly lipophilic and has a large volume of distribution (335 L). However, it has a longer and more variable CSHT due to rapid redistribution. The rapid redistribution back to plasma prevents the plasma concentration from quickly falling after the infusion is stopped, even though fentanyl is rapidly cleared (1530 mL/min). Alfentanil (purple line) has a small volume of distribution (27 L) due to a lower lipid solubility and a high degree of protein binding (90%). Since much less of the drug redistributes into peripheral tissues, redistribution back to plasma does not significantly affect plasma concentration. This explains why the CSHT of alfentanil does not increase after about two hours of infusion time. Note however for short infusions, the CSHT of alfentanil is higher than for fentanyl. This occurs since the plasma clearance of alfentanil is significantly lower (240 mL/min) than fentanyl. Remifentanil (red line) has a flat and low CSHT curve. Remifentanil’s ester structure causes it to be very rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma and tissue nonspecific esterases. Accordingly, it has a very high plasma clearance (4000 mL/min) which keeps the CSHT low. The drug’s volume of distribution is also low (30 L) so redistribution does little to raise plasma concentration after the infusion is turned off. This causes the CSHT curve to remain flat even with long-running infusions. Although not depicted on the graph, the curve for sufentanil closely resembles the propofol curve. Sufentanil’s CSHT is lower than fentanyl and alfentanil because of a moderately high plasma clearance (900 mL/min) and because of its redistribution pharmacokinetics. Sufentanil has a moderately large volume of distribution (120-250 L) and the drug slowly equilibrates between the plasma and peripheral compartments. Due to this slow equilibration, even after the infusion is turned off, a slow redistribution INTO the peripheral compartments continues to occur. This causes the drug’s CSHT to be lower than might otherwise be expected.
rationales:
This curve represents fentanyl.
Answer C: This curve represents propofol.
Answer D: This curve represents remifentanil.
bottomLine: Context-sensitive half-time describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. It reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drugs with rapid plasma clearance and a low rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a low CSHT while drugs with a slow plasma clearance and high rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a high CSHT.
references: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 156-157, 448, 469, 491-492. Hughes MA, et al. stem: A 75-year-old patient with coronary artery disease presents in septic shock. Fluids are given, and norepinephrine is started, which is rapidly titrated up to control hypotension. Which of the following is a potential mechanism for the development of myocardial ischemia in this patient with the use of norepinephrine at high doses?
explanation: Norepinephrine can cause tachycardia, reducing time in diastole. Tachycardia increases the metabolic rate of the myocardium and decreases coronary perfusion to the left ventricle, putting patients with coronary disease at risk for myocardial ischemia. In the surgical intensive care unit (SICU), cardiovascular failure is the leading cause of death. The primary goal of treating these patients is maintaining sufficient perfusion to the vital organs through adequate cardiac output and mean arterial pressure. This goal is generally obtained through the administration of fluids with inotropic agents and/or vasopressors. Commonly used vasopressors are dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, ephedrine, and vasopressin. Unfortunately, these medications can cause negative side effects. The most common side effects are ventricular ectopy and tachyarrhythmia, which is of no surprise because of the location of stimulation. Medications that have a high degree of alpha stimulation may cause an increase in pulmonary artery pressure. Dopamine can decrease gastrointestinal mucosal perfusion, and prolonged infusion can lead to a reduced serum concentration of many hormones (prolactin, human growth hormone, and thyroid hormones). In one study, patients who developed adverse cardiac events had higher catecholamine vasopressor loads. The incidence of development was almost 50% of patients studied, and the most common adverse cardiac events were new onset tachyarrhythmia, prolonged elevated heart rate, and myocardial cell damage. In this study, epinephrine and phenylephrine were associated with an increased number of adverse cardiovascular events. Adding vasopressin to the treatment plan has been shown to decrease the dose of norepinephrine required and also to decrease the risk of serious adverse events in ventilatory shock.
rationales:
A desired effect of vasopressor therapy is an increase in systemic vascular resistance, which results in an increased, not decreased, afterload. In patients with reduced cardiac function, increased afterload may lead to an increased myocardial demand that can result in ischemia and infarction. This can be difficult in patients with vasodilatory shock. The requirement to increase the mean arterial pressure to ensure adequate perfusion must be weighed against the requirement to not increase afterload above what the myocardium can tolerate.
Answer B: Norepinephrine increases both the left ventricular end-diastolic volume and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) through increased venous blood return and left ventricular contractility. An increase in LVEDP can decrease coronary perfusion pressure and reduce coronary perfusion (depending on the concurrent changes in the aortic diastolic pressure).
bottomLine: The deleterious side effects of vasopressors may result in significant morbidity and, possibly, mortality in certain patient populations. In patients with preexisting cardiac dysfunction, medication-induced tachycardia may result in increased myocardial oxygen demand and decreased supply, resulting in myocardial ischemia.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Vasopressors: Risk Of Myocardial Ischemia" Fleisher L, et al. Pharmacology and Physiology for Anesthesia. Vasopressors and inotropes. 1st edition. Schmittinger, C. Adverse cardiac events during catecholamine vasopressor therapy: a prospective observational study. Intensive Care Med. 2012 Jun;38(6):950-8.

stem: Which of the following is the site of action for tirofiban?
explanation: Tirofiban is a glycoprotein (GP) IIb-IIIa receptor inhibitor. Ordinarily, platelets do not bind to vascular endothelium. However, following vascular damage in which the extracellular matrix (ECM) of vascular endothelium is exposed, platelets undergo adhesion, activation, and aggregation. Platelet GP Ib-factor IXfactor V receptor complexes bind to vascular ECM proteins (especially von Willebrand factor, vWF) leading to platelet adhesion. Following adhesion, platelets undergo a series of biochemical and physical changes leading to platelet activation. Storage granules release a large variety of proteins (e.g. factors V and VIII, vWF, fibrinogen, ADP, ATP, calcium) that aid in hemostasis by recruiting and activating additional platelets and helping propagate the coagulation cascade. Platelets also undergo physical changes that increase their surface area and expose additional membrane phospholipids and GP platelet surface receptors. Newly exposed GP IIb/IIIa receptors are then activated by thromboxane A2. Once activated, they bind fibrinogen and allow for cross-linking with nearby platelets thus leading to platelet aggregation and, coupled with the coagulation cascade, thrombus formation. Antiplatelet drugs work primarily by decreasing platelet aggregation via one of several different mechanisms. See the table below for information on several common antiplatelet drugs. Abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban are GP IIb-IIIa receptor inhibitors and thus prevent platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. Unlike the other drugs listed above, these are only administered IV since oral forms were associated with increased mortality. Each drug has a different duration of platelet inhibition: 24-48 hours for abciximab, 2-4 hours for eptifibatide, and 4-8 hours for tirofiban.
rationales:
Dipyridamole is phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitor and adenosine reuptake inhibitor. Platelets are unable to aggregate properly when intracellular levels of cAMP are high (due to thromboxane A2 inhibition). Since PDE breaks down cAMP, its inhibition will lead to increased cAMP levels. In addition, binding of adenosine to extracellular platelet adenosine receptors leads to an elevation of intracellular cAMP concentrations. Dipyridamole blocks adenosine reuptake by platelets, erythrocytes, and vascular endothelium leading to increased extracellular concentrations which then bind to platelet receptors, impairing aggregation.
Answer B: Clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, and ticlopidine are adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor inhibitors which impair the ADP-dependent activation of the GP IIb-IIIa complex.
Answer C: Aspirin prevents platelet aggregation by irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX). This enzyme is responsible for producing prostaglandins from which thromboxane A2 is derived. Therefore, COX inhibition leads to the downstream effect of impaired aggregation due to decreased GP IIb-IIIa activation.
bottomLine: Abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban are GP IIb-IIIa receptor inhibitors that prevent platelet aggregation and thrombus formation.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be associated with extrapyramidal side effects?
explanation: Ondansetron is a serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonist with an extremely low incidence of development of extrapyramidal side effects (EPS). Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is the leading cause of delayed discharge from the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) and for unexpected admissions after ambulatory surgery. Although many medications have shown great efficacy at preventing and/or treating PONV, they are not without side effects. Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor blocker. An abundance of this receptor was identified in the area postrema and the nucleus tractus solitarius of the brainstem. These areas are emetogenic and the inhibition of serotonin receptor binding has shown great efficacy in both preventing and treating PONV. The most common side effects of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are headache, dizziness, and constipation. As of 2014, there have been only a few case reports of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists being associated with QT prolongation on ECG when administered at usual doses. The FDA has issued a warning regarding QT prolongation with an IV bolus larger than 16 mg, and the manufacturer has removed the 32 mg single-dose formulation. Although EPS were not observed in initial clinical trials (whereas they were with droperidol, metoclopramide, and promethazine), a very small number of case reports have since implicated ondansetron in causing EPS, though the incidence is extremely low. Ondansetron has no known affinity for dopamine receptors, but animal studies suggest that it may play a role in dopaminergic transmission and therefore produce dopamine receptor-mediated side effects in certain patients. Previous history of dystonic reactions or EPS with other antiemetics appears to be the biggest risk factor for development of EPS with ondansetron. Dopamine receptors are also found in the area postrema of the brainstem and antagonism of these receptors has led to improvement and prevention of PONV. Extrapyramidal side effects can be observed after central dopamine antagonism and can manifest as acute dystonia, akinesia, or akathisia, and often resemble the signs of Parkinsonism.
rationales:
Metoclopramide is a benzamide structurally related to procainamide but lacks the local anesthetic or antiarrhythmic properties. Metoclopramide antagonizes dopamine and may lead to EPS.
Answer C: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine neuroleptic medication. This class of medications has anti-nausea properties similar to metoclopramide and the butyrophenones via inhibition of dopamine receptor activation in the area postrema. They too are prone to producing EPS.
bottomLine: The area postrema of the brainstem, also known as the chemoreceptor trigger zone, contains dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, histamine, and neurokinin type 1 receptors. Antagonism of these receptors can help treat and prevent nausea. However, any medication leading to central antagonism of dopamine receptors can potentially cause EPS.
references: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 841-842. Evers, Anesthetic Pharmacology, 2nd edition, pp. 856, 860-864. Sprung J, et al. Extrapyramidal reactions to ondansetron: cross-reactivity between ondansetron and prochlorperazine? Anesth Analg. 2003 May; 96(5): 1374-1376. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "PONV Tx: Extrapyramidal Sx"

stem: Right subclavian central venous access is attempted on a patient undergoing exploratory laparotomy under general anesthesia with 75% nitrous oxide and 0.3% isoflurane. Access is unsuccessful, and the syringe fills with air during the last attempt. Which of the following events is MOST likely to occur acutely?

options.text: Immediate drop in end tidal carbon dioxide
options.html: Immediate drop in end tidal carbon dioxide

explanation: A pneumothorax, which can rapidly grow in size with nitrous oxide use, can cause difficulty with ventilation and increased peak airway pressures in intubated patients. Subclavian vein central line placement is associated with a 1-2% risk of pneumothorax. Classically, a pneumothorax can be suspected if the syringe fills with air when venous access is being attempted, indicative of lung puncture. Most patients who develop a pneumothorax due to subclavian central line placement remain asymptomatic. However, concurrent or subsequent nitrous oxide use at 75% can expand a pneumothorax to double its size in 10 minutes and triple its size in 30 minutes. This can lead to difficulty ventilating with increased peak airway pressures. In severe cases, a tension pneumothorax can develop, in which the increased intrathoracic pressure may also impede venous return, causing reduced cardiac output and hypotension. A primary concern of nitrous oxide use is its ability to expand air-filled spaces because of its greater solubility in blood compared to nitrogen. Several closed air spaces, such as the bowel and middle ear, exist in the body. Other closed cavities may occur as a result of disease or surgery, such as a pneumothorax or a craniotomy. Nitrogen in air-filled spaces cannot be removed readily via the bloodstream, but nitrous oxide easily diffuses from the blood into these spaces. Diffusion of nitrous oxide continues into these spaces until the partial pressure equals that of the blood and alveoli (i.e. until equilibrium is reached between all three compartments).
rationales:
Although an expanding pneumothorax can cause hypoxia, hypoxic gas mixtures are unlikely to occur since most anesthesia machines have proportioning systems which require a minimum amount of oxygen dialed into the total fresh gas flow (FGF). For example, if oxygen falls below 25% of FGF, the proportioning system is activated in order to reduce N2O and to maintain O2 above this safety threshold.
Answer C: A suspected air embolus would cause a large drop in end tidal CO2. Central venous access was not obtained in this case and therefore introduction of intravascular air is highly unlikely. Tension pneumothorax can decrease cardiac return and thus decrease end tidal CO2, but this would not occur acutely.
bottomLine: A gas mixture of 75% N2O can expand a pneumothorax to double its size in 10 minutes and to 3 times its size in 30 minutes.
trueLearnInsight: The volume of an air embolus causing cardiovascular collapse during the concomitant administration of N2O is less than the volume of an air embolus causing cardiovascular collapse in the absence of N2O.
